title: The Macroeconomic Effects of Gig Work: Insurance Against Labor Market Risk
affiliations: Bank of Korea

detail.title: The Macroeconomic Effects of Gig Work: Insurance Against Labor Market Risk
detail.abstract: This paper studies the macroeconomic effects of gig work, a form of platform-mediated self-employment characterized by easy entry, high turnover, and relatively low earnings. I develop a heterogeneous-agent model with search-and-matching frictions and calibrate it to U.S. data to evaluate its aggregate and distributional implications. Introducing gig work reduces unemployment by 0.7 percentage points and raises wages by improving workers' outside options. However, it also discourages vacancy creation and shifts labor toward a lower-productivity sector, reducing output per worker by 1.8 percent. Despite this productivity loss, aggregate welfare rises by about 0.7 percent. Most of the welfare gain comes from insurance: gig work allows unemployed workers to earn income while continuing to search for paid employment, smoothing consumption without fully detaching them from the labor market. The gains are largest for UI-ineligible unemployed workers and individuals with few assets. The results highlight a key trade-off: gig work acts as private income insurance for vulnerable workers, but it does so by reallocating labor toward less productive activities.

title: Tax, Wars, and the State: Political Stability in Indochinese Vietnam During 1900-1930
affiliations: Vietnam National University (VNU) - VNU University of Economics and Business

detail.title: Tax, Wars, and the State: Political Stability in Indochinese Vietnam During 1900-1930
detail.abstract: This article studies the role of tax on the Vietnamese political instability during the French colonial period. Guided by the literature and its implied theories, tax hypothetically exerts countervailing effects on the political situation. This article proceeds with the instrumental variable technique that separates and investigates the role of tax itself which is otherwise entangled in the complex structure of tax, wars, and state capacity. Finally, this article draws some implications on and revisits the theory of tax, wars, and the state. It denounces any monolithic and reductionist approaches to such complex structure.

title: The LogaNetto Model: A Fairness-Axiomatic Income Tax Tariff with Logarithmic Net Income

detail.title: The LogaNetto Model: A Fairness-Axiomatic Income Tax Tariff with Logarithmic Net Income
detail.abstract: A fair income tax can be characterised not only politically but also mathematically uniquely. Six structural fairness axioms-continuity, tariff transitivity, strict progression above a basic allowance, tax exemption below it, a maximum tax rate as asymptotic limit, and unbounded growth of net income-together with the standard assumption of logarithmic utility uniquely determine one class of tariff functions: the LogaNetto model. It is determined by three politically interpretable parameters: a basic allowance 𝐸 0 , a steepness parameter 𝑎, and a maximum tax rate t max. The marginal rate is t(E) = 0 for E ≤ E 0 and T(E) = 𝑡 max (E-E 0)/((E-E 0) + 𝑎) for E > E 0 , approaching the maximum rate T max smoothly and asymptotically without ever reaching it at any finite income; net income grows without bound, and logarithmically in the pure limiting case t max = 1. This contrasts with the seven structural parameters of the current German statutory tariff (§ 32a of the German Income Tax Act, Einkommensteuergesetz). The functional form coincides with the result obtained by Young (1990) from equal sacrifice with logarithmic utility, but the present axiomatic derivation isolates the structural fairness intuitions separately from the utility-theoretic uniqueness step. Calibrated to German income tax data for 2021, the class implies substantial middle-class relief and steeper topincome taxation than the current statutory tariff. Behavioural considerations following Saez (2001) suggest a maximum tax rate of around 63 percent for Germany.

title: Inventory Record Inaccuracy In Grocery Retailing: Impact Of Promotions And Product Perishability, And Targeted Effect Of Audits
affiliations: , Mays Business School, Texas A&M University, Cardiff University - Cardiff Business School and Technical University Darmstadt

detail.title: Inventory Record Inaccuracy In Grocery Retailing: Impact Of Promotions And Product Perishability, And Targeted Effect Of Audits
detail.abstract: We report the results of a study to identify and quantify drivers of inventory record inaccuracy (IRI) in a grocery retailing environment, a context characterized by frequent promotions and a high share of perishable items. The analysis covers ~24,000 stock keeping units (SKUs) sold in 11 stores. We find that IRI is positively associated with average inventory level, restocking frequency, and whether the item is perishable, and negatively associated with promotional activity. We also conduct a field quasi-experiment to assess the marginal effect of stockcounts on sales. While performing an inventory audit is found to lead to an 11% store-wide sales lift, the audit has heterogeneous effects with all the sales lift concentrated on items exhibiting negative IRI (i.e., where system inventory is greater than actual inventory). The benefits of inventory audits are also found to be more pronounced on perishable items, that are associated with higher IRI levels. Our findings inform retailers on the appropriate allocation of effort to improve IRI and reframe stock counting as a sales-increasing strategy rather than a cost-intensive necessity.

title: From Agglomeration Economies to Borrowed Size: Relational Scale, Network-Based Convergence, and Regional Resilience in Japan's Mature Economy

detail.title: From Agglomeration Economies to Borrowed Size: Relational Scale, Network-Based Convergence, and Regional Resilience in Japan's Mature Economy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or non-financial interests relevant to this research note.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required because this research note does not involve human participants, patient data, personal data, or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research note received no specific funding. The monograph series synthesized in this note includes research supported by previous JSPS KAKENHI grants, as acknowledged in the respective volumes.

detail.abstract: Japan presents a regional paradox: population decline and concentration in the Greater Tokyo Area continue, yet since the 2000s several measures of regional economic performance across prefectures have shown signs of convergence rather than divergence. This note interprets the paradox as a post-third stage of networkbased convergence following the Fujita-Tabuchi account of Japan's spatial development-one in which interregional networks and institutional connectivity, rather than physical deconcentration, mediate access to scale. It synthesizes a three-volume monograph series by Akihiro Otsuka as a cumulative research program moving from the productivity analysis of agglomeration economies, through interregional network economies and regional sustainability, to Borrowed Size as relational scale and regional resilience. Borrowed Size is defined not as proximity to a large metropolis but as an effective scale that a region constructs by accessing external resources through networks and converting those resources through absorptive capacity and institutional coordination. Three propositions organize the synthesis: relational scale can matter alongside size; connectivity is more likely to yield gains when aligned with absorptive and institutional capacity; and under demographic decline, interregional complementarity may offer a more appropriate alternative to simple grow-big strategies. The evidence is coherent, model-based, and associational; formal modeling, causal identification, microdata, international comparison, and a transparent Borrowed Size Index remain future tasks.

title: Is India Leapfrogging: A Technological and Environmental Analysis

detail.title: Is India Leapfrogging: A Technological and Environmental Analysis
detail.abstract: India's shift into the tertiary sector raises key questions about India's leapfrogging: [How has India utilized leapfrogging strategies to transition directly to cleaner energy sources, how and what are the advancements in India's digital infrastructure, and how has the growth of tech-based industries contributed to India's GDP. Latecomer countries often have the advantage to leapfrog over the traditional methods of development that were previously employed by other developing countries, because of already existing and pre-established technology. Therefore, since India is a latecomer in terms of development, the paper discusses whether India is leapfrogging both technologically and environmentally. The paper analyzes metrics such as clean energy adoption, CO 2 emissions per capita, digital infrastructure, and emerging technologies in its analysis. While India's environmental growth shows mixed results-adopting cleaner energy sources but with its CO 2 emissions per capita increasing-its technological advancements show signs of rapid leapfrogging, particularly in adopting technologies like IoT and AI. Additionally, this paper examines the impact of key policies implemented by the Indian government, like the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan and the National Solar Mission, in fueling its transition.

title: Pricing Carbon or Salience? Evidence from Cryptocurrency Markets
affiliations: Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge

detail.title: Pricing Carbon or Salience? Evidence from Cryptocurrency Markets
detail.abstract: In equity markets, separating environmental salience from carbon transition risk is a central identification challenge, as carbon pricing attributed to investor preferences may instead reflect hedging of future carbon liabilities. I address this problem by exploiting cryptocurrency markets, where investors do not face any carbon liability. Using a nature-driven exogenous shock to carbon footprint, I show that investors ignore its predictable changes and do not price carbon. However, they react sharply to attention shocks that make carbon salient. My findings speak directly to a central debate on investor preferences and address a major identification problem in the carbon-pricing literature.

title: Reproducibility is the New Copyleft: Defining AGI-oriented Reproducible Builds

detail.title: Reproducibility is the New Copyleft: Defining AGI-oriented Reproducible Builds

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by JSPS KAKENHI Grant Number 26K15531.

detail.abstract: The concept of copyleft, as implemented in licenses such as the GNU General Public License, was a legal hack that used copyright to guarantee user freedom by tying the availability of source code to every act of distribution. Its normative force rested on an implicit technical premise: that source code and object code stand in a well-defined, humanly auditable, and reproducible relationship. Large language models and, prospectively, Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) systems systematically violate this premise. The training artifacts jointly required to reconstruct a given model-code, data, weights, hyperparameters, toolchain, and hardware configuration-are each subject to independent legal, technical, and economic constraints that no current open-source framework fully resolves. Sufficiently capable AI systems can also rewrite licensed source into functionally equivalent derivatives stripped of their original obligations, a form of laundering against which copyleft has no effective defense. This paper argues that a functional analogue of copyleft for AGI must be grounded not in share-alike clauses over code, but in reproducible builds: a practice guaranteeing bit-exact reconstructability from declared inputs. We review the history and logic of copyleft, critically examine Maffulli's Second Liberation thesis according to which AI fulfills Stallman's dream, and show that the argument collapses unless AGI systems are themselves reproducible. Drawing on the Open Source AI Definition (OSAID), the Model Openness Framework (MOF), OpenMDW, and deterministicinference research by Thinking Machines Lab, SGLang, and others, we define seven requirements for AGI-oriented reproducible builds. We further argue that the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and analogous AIto-AI coupling mechanisms constitute a new dynamic linking layer for which copyleft-style licensing is ill-suited, and that Masnick's "protocols, not platforms" framework offers a more promising governance template for the AI linking layer.

title: Human Development And The Asymmetry Of Economic Growth

detail.title: Human Development And The Asymmetry Of Economic Growth
detail.abstract: Our objective is to explain human development in the Peruvian economy for the period 1990 − 2021 using nonlinear auto-regressive distributed lag (NARDL) models. We present empirical evidence supporting the hypothesis that there is a mixed long-term relationship. We find an asymmetric impact, both positive and negative, between human development levels and per capita income, with coefficients of +0.18 and −1.38, respectively. Furthermore, we have strong empirical evidence supporting the hypothesis that economic growth, in its negative component lagged by one period, explains the growth in human development, reflecting a positive and statistically significant causal relationship at the 1 % level, with a coefficient of +0.32. In addition, evidence is presented showing symmetrical impacts that explain human development, such as unequal income distribution (−0.04), lagged ecological footprint (+0.08), COVID (−0.09), and institutional factors (+0.01), which are statistically significant at the 5 % level.

title: The Geopolitics of Cryptography: End-to-End Encryption at the Intersection of Technology, Security, and Sovereignty

detail.title: The Geopolitics of Cryptography: End-to-End Encryption at the Intersection of Technology, Security, and Sovereignty

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that he has no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, human subjects, animals, or personal data. It is based entirely on the analysis of publicly available primary sources, legal and policy documents, and secondary literature. Ethics approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by JSPS KAKENHI Grant Number 26K15531.

detail.abstract: End-to-end encryption (E2EE) has become a central site of conflict among privacy rights, national security, and digital sovereignty. This paper integrates comparative policy analysis, technical feasibility assessment, and multi-stakeholder analysis to examine the international dynamics of E2EE regulation across twenty jurisdictions. It develops an original five-part typology-prohibitionist, conditional-access, permissive, hybrid, and network-shutdowndependent-and argues that regulatory divergence is shaped less by technical constraints than by how digital sovereignty is conceptualized, the character of political regimes, and institutional linkages with the lawful-interception industry. The paper further demonstrates that backdoor demands have persisted for thirty years despite their technical infeasibility. This persistence is explained by a self-reinforcing cycle in which organizational reputation maintenance, security-industry interests, and political framing around child protection and counterterrorism mutually reinforce each other. Platform companies are repositioned as quasi-sovereign actors whose norm-making capacity over encrypted digital communications rivals that of states. These private entities exercise strategic resistance through technical architecture and cryptographic discourse, doing so selectively as a function of market scale and state coercive capacity.

title: Network-Based Monetary Theory: Conceptual Foundations, Variable Philosophy, and the Case for a New Monetary Framework Why Verified Human Networks May Constitute a New Monetary Variable -Before the Mathematics
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Network-Based Monetary Theory: Conceptual Foundations, Variable Philosophy, and the Case for a New Monetary Framework Why Verified Human Networks May Constitute a New Monetary Variable -Before the Mathematics

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper. This research was conducted independently without any institutional or commercial bias.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study is purely theoretical and conceptual in nature, and does not involve any human participants, animals, or clinical data requiring ethical approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. It was entirely self-funded by the author.

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces the conceptual foundations of Network-Based Monetary Theory (NBMT), a proposed framework for analyzing monetary systems that may emerge from digitally verified human networks rather than from sovereign issuance alone.

Existing monetary theories — including classical quantity theory (Fisher, 1911), Keynesian demand frameworks (Keynes, 1936), Hayekian competitive currency theory (Hayek, 1976), and Modern Monetary Theory (Wray, 2012) — share a common implicit assumption: that settlement infrastructure is stable, neutral, and operationally available. NBMT proposes that this assumption is increasingly insufficient. Between 2023 and 2026, the global monetary environment demonstrated that settlement systems, digital identity infrastructure, and geopolitical exposure have themselves become active monetary variables — evidenced by the enactment of the GENIUS Act (July 2025), the full implementation of MiCA (December 2024), the weaponization of SWIFT (2022), the targeting of financial infrastructure during the March 2026 Gulf crisis, and the UAE's exit from OPEC (May 2026).

This paper serves a specific purpose within the research series: it establishes the conceptual architecture that Paper IV formalizes mathematically. For each variable introduced in the formal framework — including the Verified Participant Ratio (ρ_v), Economic Activity Ratio (α_e), Real Asset Integration Ratio (σ_r), External Risk Coefficient (R_ext), Network Topology Coefficient (β), and the composite Network Sovereignty Index (V_s) — this paper clarifies the underlying economic logic, functional interpretation, methodological rationale, and the alternative definition that was considered and rejected. Variables are further classified by observational status: Observable, Partially Observable, or Latent Composite, with direct implications for how each may be tested or falsified.

The paper establishes the theoretical distinction between V_s as a structural monetary variable and purely descriptive index construction. It presents five falsifiable predictions — covering settlement stability, adoption dynamics, geopolitical resilience, crisis pricing, and cross-border adoption — each with an explicit falsification condition. It addresses four structural limitations: the Oracle Problem, the Seigniorage Problem, the Hoarding Problem, and the Governance Problem.

NBMT does not predict the replacement of sovereign monetary systems. Its central, testable claim is narrower: if verified human networks become increasingly responsible for cross-border settlement and economic coordination, then traditional monetary variables alone may become insufficient to explain monetary stability, adoption dynamics, and settlement resilience.

title: Categorical Thinking over Continuous Attributes and Firm Pricing
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Categorical Thinking over Continuous Attributes and Firm Pricing
detail.abstract: Round-number price discontinuities in market data are a leading piece of evidence for consumer inattention. They are equally consistent with categorical thinking, consumers grouping a continuous attribute like mileage into discrete buckets ("low-mileage" versus "high-mileage"), with valuation drops at the boundaries between categories. Price data alone cannot separate the two. This paper introduces an external measure that separates categorization from a parsimonious inattention benchmark. Using large language models, I extract category boundaries from millions of online vehicle discussions and merge them with millions of Texas used-car transactions. The externally measured boundary prevalence predicts cross-make heterogeneity in transaction-price discontinuities that a parsimonious inattention model with one bias parameter per digit position cannot generate, and the prediction survives after absorbing positionspecific above-cutoff effects at 10k and 100k multiples. A 10-percentage-point increase in prevalence is associated with a 1.04-percentage-point larger listing-price drop and a 1.23-percentage-point larger transaction-price drop at the cutoff. On the firm side, the listing-to-transaction pass-through ratio rises from 81% in the lowest-prevalence quintile to 83% in the highest, and days on lot lengthen at high prevalence boundaries. The joint pattern rejects optimal pricing under categorical demand and points to dealers under-calibrating to cutoff-specific prevalence. Firms can improve profits by conditioning posted prices on the same categorical prevalence that identifies the consumer-side mechanism.

title: Creative Destruction, Diffusion of Technology, and Differential Profit Rates: A Classical-Evolutionary Analysis

detail.title: Creative Destruction, Diffusion of Technology, and Differential Profit Rates: A Classical-Evolutionary Analysis
detail.abstract: This paper develops an analytical microfoundation for the persistence of inter-sectoral profit rate differentials and the countervailing character of capital mobility, integrating the classical long-period method with an evolutionary framework of creative destruction and technology diffusion. The classical competition hypothesis posits that free capital mobility across sectors generates a long-run tendency toward a uniform profit rate. While this tendency has been extensively formalized in the modern classical tradition, the existing literature lacks a microfoundation linking the evolutionary dynamics of innovation to the structure of profit rate differentials. We develop a two-sector model with heterogeneous, boundedly rational firms. Within the innovating sector, technology diffusion proceeds through differential profit rates, progressively reducing average production conditions and reducing the relative price of the capital good, thereby generating an inter-sectoral profit rate differential. The capital mobility response is structurally countervailing: adopters intensify investment in the innovating sector while non-adopters, whose returns are compressed by the price decline, exit or imitate. These opposing flows weaken the aggregate equalizing force relative to standard classical models. Three findings follow. First, intra-sectoral diffusion generates inter-sectoral differentials even without barriers to capital mobility. Second, the mobility response is countervailing between adopter and non-adopter, rendering equalization strictly slower than the classical benchmark. Third, under continuous innovations, differentials are endogenously reproduced before preceding adjustments completion, so that profit rate equalization is a conditional tendency perpetually deferred by the dynamics of creative destruction.

title: Batch Prediction Auctions with a Scalar Dual Reduction
affiliations: Independent and Independent

detail.title: Batch Prediction Auctions with a Scalar Dual Reduction
detail.abstract: We introduce Batch Prediction Auctions (BPA), a batch-cleared parimutuel mechanism for prediction markets. We show that the clearing problem admits a scalar dual reduction, transforming the multi-dimensional equilibrium problem into a one-dimensional root-finding task. The resulting mechanism is deterministic, self-financing, and requires no liquidity providers. This formulation yields a simple and efficient batchclearing algorithm suitable for prediction markets and on-chain implementation.

title: Re-examination of Influencer Popularity-Purchase Intention Relationship in Live Streaming
affiliations: Universiti Putra Malaysia, Universiti Putra Malaysia and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Re-examination of Influencer Popularity-Purchase Intention Relationship in Live Streaming
detail.abstract: Abstract: This study aims to examine the relationship between Influencer Popularity (IP) and Live Purchase Intention (LPI) in the context of live streaming by operationalizing both constructs as multidimensional constructs. In contrast to previous studies that typically measure popularity based solely on follower count and purchase intention unidimensionally, this study integrates quantitative dimensions (follower size and likes), reputation legitimacy (non-controversial image, well-known), and aspirational appeal (likable, exemplary) for IP, as well as urgency, frequency, increased spending, channel preference, and advocacy dimensions for LPI. This study uses a deductive approach with a cross-sectional design. Data were collected from 230 female respondents in mainland China who had experience watching live streaming of beauty products. Analysis was conducted using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) via SmartPLS 3.3.9. The results showed that Influencer Popularity had a positive and significant relationship with Live Purchase Intention (β = 0.432, t = 6.448, p < 0.001). This finding suggests that popularity functions as a social signal that can increase purchase urgency, spending intensity, and advocacy propensity. Theoretically, this study enriches the influencer marketing literature by proposing a more comprehensive multidimensional framework consistent with the dynamic nature of live streaming commerce. From a practical perspective, this study emphasizes the importance of selecting influencers based on a combination of visibility, reputation legitimacy, and aspirational appeal to maximize the effectiveness of marketing strategies in the real-time digital commerce ecosystem.

title: Chronos-vs. Kairos-Framed Pitches: Evidence of A Seesaw Effect from Observational, Experimental, and Neurophysiological Analyses
affiliations: Lanzhou University, , University of Florida - Warrington College of Business Administration, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Xidian University and University of Iowa

detail.title: Chronos-vs. Kairos-Framed Pitches: Evidence of A Seesaw Effect from Observational, Experimental, and Neurophysiological Analyses
detail.abstract: Live-streaming platforms offer influencers a powerful stage to engage consumers emotionally. While narrative language structured through storytelling is known to deepen engagement, many influencers instead favor assertive, urgent language. To reconcile this empirical tension, we investigate both the current sales impact and the downstream consequences of different sales pitches by introducing a novel temporal framing perspective that distinguishes between Chronos (time as linear duration) and Kairos (time as decisive moments). Our results reveal a compelling seesaw effect: Chronos framing enhances downstream sales but is less effective at driving immediate purchases, whereas Kairos framing increases immediate conversions but does so at the expense of subsequent sales. This asymmetry is validated in three randomized online experiments, one of which uses AI-generated, tone-cloned live-streaming clips, and it remains robust after scarcity cues, herding effects, and differences in products and influencers are accounted for. Complementing the behavioral evidence, electroencephalography data reveal the underlying neurophysiological mechanisms. Chronos framing elicits greater left-hemispheric activation, which is linked to approach motivation and sustained, goal-directed attention, facilitating deeper cognitive processing. Kairos framing triggers stronger right-hemispheric activation, which is indicative of withdrawal-oriented affect, emotional vigilance, and reactive attention, supporting rapid decisions but potentially depleting cognitive resources and reducing receptivity to subsequent products. Our findings extend temporal framing theory and offer actionable guidance for optimizing persuasive flows in live commerce.

title: When Is a Composite Response a Structural Primitive?

detail.title: When Is a Composite Response a Structural Primitive?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is theoretical and uses only publicly available, de-identified data for an illustrative diagnostic. It did not involve human participants, animals, or personal data requiring ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: A local response is often used as if it were a structural primitive: observe how behavior moves under one incentive, then ask what would happen under another. This paper asks when that step is valid. The di!culty is that an observed response is a composite of productivity, cost, measurement, and capacity primitives. It remains a faithful object only on domains where those primitives move together. At a frontier-a capacity limit, an eligibility threshold, or a notch-the response can fan out into distinct components and stop supporting the counterfactual. I characterize the response's validity domain, the counterfactuals that survive after fan-out, and the minimal regime information that restores a point answer. The framework is a triage step between the general Lucas warning and bespoke structural modeling: a pre-structural diagnostic for fan-out, a specification-free identified set for what survives, and the least extra object that repairs the counterfactual. A public-data diagnostic at the conforming-loan limit, where a documented response is known to be composite, illustrates how the object is visible in administrative data.

title: Digital Financial Trust and Financial Resilience: Evidence from a Pilot Survey of UPI Users in India

detail.title: Digital Financial Trust and Financial Resilience: Evidence from a Pilot Survey of UPI Users in India
detail.abstract: India's Unified Payments Interface (UPI) has expanded real-time digital payment access across diverse population segments, yet access alone does not ensure meaningful financial inclusion. This paper examines whether digital financial trust, perceived risk, financial literacy, transaction-value sensitivity, and redressal confidence are associated with high-value UPI adoption and financial resilience. Using 300 survey responses from UPI users across India, we test a Value Elasticity of Digital Trust model extending the Technology Acceptance Model with institutional trust variables. Results show redressal confidence (β=0.388, p<0.001) is the strongest predictor of financial resilience, outperforming perceived ease of use, subjective norm, and financial literacy. Willingness to rely on UPI contracts sharply as transaction stakes increase — even among experienced, high-frequency users. We term this the value elasticity of digital trust and demonstrate that it is moderated by institutional responsiveness rather than technological familiarity. Findings have implications for digital retail service design, consumer protection policy, and the institutional conditions enabling sustained digital field.

title: Learning from Rare Clicks: A Comparative Study of Imbalance-Handling Techniques For Deep CTR Prediction
affiliations: Boğaziçi University, Boğaziçi University and Boğaziçi University

detail.title: Learning from Rare Clicks: A Comparative Study of Imbalance-Handling Techniques For Deep CTR Prediction
detail.abstract: Click-through Rate (CTR) prediction is an essential but difficult task in online advertising and recommendation systems. The imbalanced nature of click data, where positive click instances are much fewer in number than non-click instances, is one of the major issues in this task. This work presents an extensive comparison of rare event handling methods combined with three state-of-the-art deep learning models for CTR prediction tasks, namely, Deep and Cross Network (DCN), Deep Factorization Machine (DeepFM), and Deep Neural Network (DNN). The rare event handling methods being considered are data-level methods such as Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) and NearMiss undersampling, and algorithm-level methods such as class weight, PolyLoss, and Dice loss functions. The experiments are conducted on two large real-world datasets: the Avazu CTR prediction dataset, containing 1.4 million training samples and a CTR of 16.16 percent; and the Trendyol JFY Ads dataset, a 5 million training sample dataset provided by the company Trendyol, an e-commerce company, where the CTR is around 5 percent.  The experimental results, validated through multi-seed Wilcoxon signed-rank tests ($n = 7$, $p < 0.05$), show that PolyLoss achieves the best mean AUC on Avazu (0.7675 with DNN, +0.44\% over baseline) and on Trendyol (0.6710 with DCN, +0.56\% over baseline). These results demonstrate that algorithm-level methods show greater consistency in performance improvements across diverse datasets and models, compared to data-level approaches.

title: Deep Learning in Electronic Financial Markets: A Wavelet-LSTM Algorithmic Trading System for the Lead-Lag Effect
affiliations: Hebei University of Economics and Business

detail.title: Deep Learning in Electronic Financial Markets: A Wavelet-LSTM Algorithmic Trading System for the Lead-Lag Effect
detail.abstract: We investigate the non-linear dynamics of the lead-lag effect generated by delayed information transfers between large-cap and small-cap equities. A Composite Leadership Score, introduced to delineate leader and follower portfolios, and daily data from the Shanghai Stock Exchange's top 300 firms (2016–2025) serve as the foundation for our empirical tests. Traditional linear econometrics fail to detect these latent flows. We propose a Wavelet-LSTM architecture. By employing MODWT to filter microstructural noise without look-ahead bias, we extract purified orthogonal signals. These are then processed by an LSTM network optimized via a Huber loss function, allowing our model to successfully forecast out-of-sample returns (0.74% MAE). The resulting active trading strategy produces a 17.04% annualized return and a 0.986 Sharpe ratio. This significant outperformance against the buy-and-hold benchmark remains intact even when applying a strict 0.50% round-trip transaction cost. The integration of wavelet filtering with deep learning frameworks amplifies the extraction of latent signals from market noise, providing a highly robust algorithmic trading system.

title: Unintended Consequences of Recommender System Interventions: Evidence from a Field Experiment
affiliations: Washington University in St. Louis - John M. Olin Business School,  and Washington University in St. Louis - John M. Olin Business School

detail.title: Unintended Consequences of Recommender System Interventions: Evidence from a Field Experiment
detail.abstract: Platform content interventions in recommendation systems are typically evaluated as static "nudges," ignoring that the systems adaptively learn from the resulting user behavior. We investigate this dynamic through a large-scale field experiment on a short-video platform. The experiment involves a "sleep reminder" campaign designed to reduce late-night usage. Paradoxically, the intervention increased late-night engagement by 14.75% and overall platform usage by 2.18%, and the effects persisted for weeks even after the experiment. We explain this through a forced-exploration mechanism, showing that by revealing high latent demand for the promoted content, the intervention triggers a recommendation policy update that routine user behavior would not produce. The data generated by the intervention induced the algorithm to update its post-campaign policy, reinforcing the very engagement loops the campaign aimed to mitigate. Our findings demonstrate that user-facing interventions can effectively retrain the underlying algorithm, triggering durable, system-wide shifts in content distribution that challenge standard evaluation metrics in platform governance and social responsibility initiatives.

title: CogniGraph: Governed Graph-of-Agents Reasoning over Knowledge Graph Topologies with Semantic SHACL Validation and Constrained F1 Evaluation
affiliations: Quantamix Solutions B.V

detail.title: CogniGraph: Governed Graph-of-Agents Reasoning over Knowledge Graph Topologies with Semantic SHACL Validation and Constrained F1 Evaluation
detail.abstract: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems are increasingly deployed for regulatory and high-stakes reasoning, yet none of the prevailing flat-topology frameworks-AutoGen, CrewAI, LangGraph-enforce semantic governance over what each agent may say, in whose name, and within which scope. The result is what we term ungoverned creativity at scale: plausible-sounding answers that mix regulatory provisions, misattribute framework requirements, or drift beyond an agent's intended boundary. We ask: can a knowledge graph itself act as the coordination substrate of a multi-agent reasoning system, and can semantic validation gates supply the governance guarantees that the EU AI Act mandates? We present CogniGraph, a Graph-of-Agents framework in which each activated node of a domain knowledge graph hosts an autonomous LLM agent, communication follows the graph's typed edge topology via convergent message passing, and a SemanticSHACLGate enforces three-layer semantic validation-framework fidelity, scope boundary, and cross-reference integrity-on every agent output. A Prize-Collecting Steiner Tree (PCST) sub-graph activation step bounds per-query reasoning cost at O(|V * |•R) independently of |V |; a zero-inference-cost MasterObserver provides complete provenance traces; and the system is evaluated using a new joint quality-governance metric, Constrained F1. On MultiGov-30, a 30-question multi-regulation EU governance benchmark spanning the AI Act, GDPR, DORA, and NIS2, CogniGraph (Semantic-SHACL) achieves Constrained F1 of 0.756 against 0.328 for an ungoverned single-agent Claude Sonnet 4.6 baseline (+130%), with governance accuracy of 99.4% (framework fidelity 100%, scope adherence 100%, cross-reference integrity 98.3%). The transition from format-based to semantic SHACL validation independently lifted token F1 by 18% (0.437 → 0.517) by eliminating 49% false-rejection of correct answers. CogniGraph is distributed as the open-source GraQle SDK (pip install graqle, CLI graq); the MultiGov-30 benchmark, the SemanticSHACLGate specification, and the full reference implementation are released under Apache 2.0 to enable independent replication. 1

title: The Future of Pan-African Banking Digital Finance, Cross-Border Payments, and Financial Inclusion Under AfCFTA

detail.title: The Future of Pan-African Banking Digital Finance, Cross-Border Payments, and Financial Inclusion Under AfCFTA
detail.abstract: Africa's banking sector stands at a defining inflection point. The convergence of AfCFTA, rapid fintech adoption, expanding mobile money ecosystems, and the operationalization of the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS) is reshaping financial services across the continent's 54 economies. For the first time in Africa's economic history, a coherent infrastructure exists - or is being built - to support true pan-African financial integration. Sub-Saharan Africa's financial inclusion rate has risen from 23% in 2011 to 49% in 2024, driven predominantly by mobile money platforms such as M-Pesa, MTN Mobile Money, and Orange Money. Yet Africa remains one of the world's most expensive regions for cross-border transactions, with average remittance costs exceeding 8.2% - nearly three times the G20-mandated target of 3%. This structural inefficiency costs African economies an estimated $12–15 billion annually. The AfCFTA, operational since January 2021 with 54 signatory states, creates an unprecedented opportunity to grow intra-African trade from roughly $192 billion annually to over $440 billion by 2035. Realizing that potential requires simultaneous modernization of banking infrastructure, payment systems, regulatory frameworks, and financial supervision architectures.

title: Who Delivers Better Coupons? Higher-Preference vs. Lower-Preference E-Commerce Platforms in Competitive Equilibrium
affiliations: Chongqing Technology and Business University, Chongqing Technology and Business University, Sichuan International Studies University and Chongqing Technology and Business University

detail.title: Who Delivers Better Coupons? Higher-Preference vs. Lower-Preference E-Commerce Platforms in Competitive Equilibrium
detail.abstract: This study delves into an analysis of coupon promotion strategies employed by e-commerce platforms in a competitive environment. A supply chain consisting of one manufacturer and two competitive e-commerce platforms with different consumer preference levels is considered. The manufacturer leverages both platforms simultaneously to distribute its products, while the platforms utilize coupons as a strategic tool to attract potential customers. To unravel the intricacies of these couponing strategies, four coupon promotion models are developed and compared. The main results are obtained as follows: (1) the higher-preference e-platform, under intense competition, will fall into the Chicken Game scenario; under moderate competition, it should offer coupons; and under low competition, it should not. (2) The lower-preference e-platform will also fall into the Chicken Game under fierce competition, otherwise, it should offer coupons. (3) When both platforms offer coupons, the manufacturer experiences the most favorable outcomes in terms of both sales volume and profitability. (4) Consumers reap the highest benefits when both e-commerce platforms engage in coupon promotions. (5) In the case of intense e-platform competition, it is best for social welfare when both platforms offer coupons; otherwise, it is best when no coupons are offered.

title: Breaking AI Collusion with Consumer AI
affiliations: and

detail.title: Breaking AI Collusion with Consumer AI
detail.abstract: There is sufficient evidence in both the academic literature and the popular press that machine learning algorithms can collude. When firms price their products using machine learning algorithms, the algorithms can, after several interactions, determine that a collusive price is the best price. In this paper, we use a gametheoretic model to study methods for breaking AI collusion. Much of the discussion of algorithmic collusion centers on the collusion among producer-side algorithms. However, the use of AI on the consumer side is also rapidly growing, especially with the rise of Agentic AI. Many consumers increasingly delegate product search, comparison, and purchase decisions to consumer-facing AI agents, such as the ChatGPT agent and Amazon's Alexa shopping assistant. We propose a method in which such consumer AI providers can strategically inject demand noise into the market to break collusion. The consumer AI can do this by randomizing the purchases of a small fraction of subscribed consumers. The collusion of producer-side algorithms heavily relies on their ability to monitor each other's actions and tacitly punish (by undercutting the price) if any collusive partner deviates from the collusive price. Strategically induced demand noise hampers this monitoring ability and makes it easy for producer firms to deviate from collusion without being detected by the rival (due to noise); thus, it breaks the collusion by incentivizing deviation from it. We establish the robustness of this method when the producer-side algorithms strategically react to such noise injection. We also analyze how strategic adoption of AI by consumers affects the effectiveness of our method and characterize the conditions under which the method continues to break collusion. We find that although the objective of consumer AI providers is to maximize their own profits instead of maximizing consumer surplus, their presence always increases consumer surplus due to the breaking of collusion. Our analysis also reveals how the demand noise can be optimally designed depending on the market characteristics to increase the chances of breaking collusion. Our results contribute to the ongoing debate on algorithmic collusion and provide policy recommendations.

title: Programming a Biological Cell: a review
affiliations: University College London, University of College London, University of College London and BITS, Pilani

detail.title: Programming a Biological Cell: a review

declarations.ethicsApproval: NA
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: This paper reviews research into programming a biological cell (e.g. synthetic biology) treating cells like "codeable" machines. For biology, arguably, the endpoint is what we refer to as a DNAprogrammable biological microcomputer (Treleaven, 2021; Treleaven & Schoernig, 2025): a genetic engineering tool analogous to CRISPR (Thurtle-Schmidt & Lo, 2018) or Evo 2 (Evo 2, 2025). Notably, a cell comes with all the "hardware" and the information processing mechanisms. The challenge is creating the DNA, RNA and protein strands to "program" the cell. Currently, machine learning (ML) is driving advances in synthetic biology through strands' decoding, DNA editing, and Biological LLMs. As a case study, we present BioVibe, a working prototype Vibe coding environment for biological programming. BioVibe illustrates the development of a web-based platform (Node.js/Express) that connects a Groq-hosted LLM (LLaMA 3.3-70B) to seven live biological databases via Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool-calling: UniProt, PDB, KEGG, PubMed, the iGEM Registry, NVIDIA BioNeMo Evo 2, and a built-in Sequence-level engine. Scientists interact through natural language to design genetic circuits and select BioBrick parts. To generate and validate DNA sequences, BioVibe uses a layered sequence strategy: verified BioBrick sequences are fetched from the iGEM Registry, codon optimization is handled by CodonTransformer, and Evo 2 is reserved only for novel sequences with no registry equivalent, exploring the cell-as-computer analogy-all within a single integrated environment. For BioVibe to be a "real" genetic engineering tool it will need to include a measure of DNA "quality", and also to incorporate AI "guardrails" (Mishra, 2025) for "governance". This paper is targeted at computer scientists and laypersons interested in programmable biology (indepth knowledge of genetics is not a prerequisite). Its contribution is fourfold: ▪ "Codeable cells": to introduce biological information processing using computer science terminology. ▪ Programmable biology: to review the wealth of AI-driven research in programmable and synthetic cell biology, which treats cells as "programmable" machines. ▪ Vibe coding: to provide a general introduction to Vibe coding. ▪ BioVibe: as a case study, the design and implementation of BioVibe, a Vibe coding environment (cf. Claude Code) for programming cells is presented. BioVibe implements the four-layer Vibe architecture described in this paper-Intent, Translation, Execution, and Verification-as a functional web application with live connections to biological databases and AI models.

detail.title: Inside the Odds

detail.abstract:
Here is the abstract trimmed to land at 5,000 characters while changing as little as possible:

Prediction markets have rapidly moved from regulatory fringe to consequential financial infrastructure, yet the doctrinal and empirical foundations for governing insider trading in these markets remain underdeveloped. This Article argues that the mainstreaming of prediction markets, accelerated by shifts in administrative law and judicial decisions permitting regulated platforms to expand, has produced insider trading risks that neither securities law nor gambling law is equipped to address. Those risks became concrete in January 2026, when a Polymarket trade placed shortly before the U.S. military detention of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, and later geopolitical wagers tied to escalation risks involving Iran, triggered allegations of trading on privileged information and immediate legislative scrutiny. The episode exposed the absence of a coherent legal framework governing informational trading, compounded by ongoing uncertainty over classification. Although prediction markets operate as event contracts under the Commodity Exchange Act within the jurisdiction of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, state courts have increasingly treated them as unlicensed sports wagering, prompting the CFTC in February 2026 to announce that it would defend federally regulated platforms against state enforcement. Yet existing antifraud and material nonpublic information doctrines, developed for securities markets, do not clearly apply to trading on privileged information about real-world events. As a result, platforms such as Kalshi and Polymarket have assumed responsibility for policing insider trading through private governance, functioning as de facto regulators and increasingly formalizing insider trading prohibitions through internal rulemaking without clear statutory standards. Platform sanctions, state-level restrictions, and formal CFTC enforcement guidance in early 2026 confirm that insider trading concerns are no longer hypothetical. In June 2026, Kalshi announced mandatory employment verification for traders in high-risk markets, a six-factor risk-scoring system applied to every proposed market before listing, and platform-embedded whistleblower tools allowing users to report suspicious activity in real time, demonstrating that private governance is actively evolving in response to enforcement pressure and regulatory scrutiny.

This Article presents a systematic study of whether regulators and stakeholders recognized insider trading risks in prediction markets before they materialized. It analyzes public comments submitted to the CFTC's 2024 Notice of Proposed Rulemaking using LLM analysis, computational text analysis, and multi-model validation. The findings show that neither regulators nor commenters meaningfully engaged with insider trading risks before they became controversial, revealing a systematic failure of regulatory processes to anticipate informational abuse. Regulatory discourse focused on jurisdictional classification and definitional questions while largely ignoring informational asymmetries that enable insider trading, demonstrating that regulatory frameworks are structurally reactive. The study further shows that market participants cannot be relied upon to identify insider trading risks, undermining disclosure-centered approaches that assume informed, self-policing participation. Building on these findings, the Article develops a typology of insider trading-like misconduct, including trading based on privileged institutional access, temporal informational advantages, manipulation of event probabilities, exploitation of platform design features, and self-referential trading. It situates these practices within existing antifraud and material nonpublic information doctrines and demonstrates that current law fails to clearly prohibit key forms of informational exploitation. Because prediction markets transform informational asymmetries regarding legal, political, and state action into tradable financial assets, failure to address insider trading risks threatens market integrity, institutional legitimacy, and the credibility of probabilistic forecasting as a public information tool. The Article concludes by proposing a governance framework integrating doctrinal clarification, regulatory oversight, and platform-level safeguards before these markets fully integrate into financial and legal systems.

title: Return-Aware Platform Experimentation: New Directions for Research
affiliations: Spotify, , Spotify, California State Polytechnic University, San Luis Obispo - Orfalea College of Business, Spotify, Spotify and Spotify

detail.title: Return-Aware Platform Experimentation: New Directions for Research

declarations.declarationOfInterest: All authors except Author 4 are employees of Spotify. The manuscript underwent standard internal review for compliance and accuracy. All authors declare no additional competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: The work was supported exclusively by Spotify as part of the authors’ normal employment. No external funding was received.

detail.abstract: Platform companies run thousands of online randomized experiments ("A/B tests") internally each year to test product innovations and decide which ones to roll out to their users. A systematic literature review finds that the vast majority of relevant research since 2000 has focused on questions around statistical inference within individual experiments, rather than on maximizing returns from many experiments. This paper proposes new research directions to bring the latter perspective to fruition. We anchor our proposals in the recent return-aware framework, which treats experimentation as a resource-allocation decision problem: given a finite user base and a set of possible ideas for innovations, how should a firm allocate experimentation effort and make rollout decisions to maximize expected returns? We outline two research directions not captured by the theoretical framework. The first concerns the statistical evidence and priors that enter decision-making, focusing on the use of non-experimental signals to pre-screen ideas for A/B testing and on how to account for ex-ante unknown errors in A/B tests themselves. We discuss partial identification as a promising approach. The second concerns frictions that arise when organizations aim to implement return-maximizing decision rules, including congestion and diminished user experience from frequent product innovations, as well as misaligned incentives between decentralized product teams and the organization's objectives. We call for research clarifying or resolving these frictions. Our aim is to inspire academic and industry research on how to align the practice of internal experimentation on platforms with intended business objectives, drawing upon concepts from statistics and economics.

title: Feature-based Dynamic Matching in the Dark
affiliations: Yale University

detail.title: Feature-based Dynamic Matching in the Dark
detail.abstract: We study a distribution-agnostic variant of the feature-based dynamic matching problem, where a set of supply units must be matched immediately and irrevocably to sequentially arriving demand units. Both sides are drawn i.i.d. from possibly different distributions over high-dimensional feature vectors, and the value of a match is a function of the two vectors. We measure performance by regret, the additive loss relative to the limiting hindsight-optimal match value. State-of-the-art algorithms for this problem require accurate knowledge of the demand distribution; we show that under model misspecification their performance can be highly sub-optimal. We develop ROAR, a completely distribution-agnostic algorithm that uses only the realized demand stream itself to make forward-looking assignment decisions. ROAR requires neither knowledge of the demand distribution nor any historical demand traces. We prove an exact identity expressing the average match value under ROAR as a folded average of hindsight-optimal values. As a consequence, ROAR obtains the same near-optimal regret scalings as the state-of-the-art algorithms that know the demand distribution exactly, across broad classes of quality functions and distributions.

title:
Democratizing Skills and the Superstar Effect:
A Theory of Technological Tipping Points in Wages
affiliations: and

detail.title:
Democratizing Skills and the Superstar Effect:
A Theory of Technological Tipping Points in Wages
detail.abstract: U.S. wage inequality rose sharply from 1980 to 2000 and then slowed, while technological diffusion did not. I develop an assignment model in which technology shifts a marketclearing ability threshold 𝑥 * (𝐾), partitioning workers into a compression regime (𝛽 < 1) and an amplification regime (𝛾 > 1). The central theoretical result is closed-form: the betweengroup variance 𝐵(𝑝) = 𝑝(1-𝑝)Δ(𝑝) 2 has a unique interior maximizer 𝑝 * 𝐵 ∈ (1/2, 1), so the growth rate of inequality is single-peaked in the share below threshold, and a risingfrontier new-task channel delays long-run reversion. Three NLSY79 findings support the mechanism: within-occupation slope ratios 𝛾 𝑗 > 𝛽 𝑗 in 8 of 8 broad sectors (ratios 1.77-11.93); within-AFQT-decile wage variance growth of +1.35%/yr (wild cluster bootstrap 𝑝 = 0.003), inside the prespecified identity-𝑊 band; and asymmetric upper-tail dispersion, which no named rival predicts. A within-U.S. state-Bartik inverted-U at β2 =-0.39 (twoway clustered 𝑝 = 0.025, pre-trends placebo 𝑝 = 0.988) provides the causal identification.

title: Data-Driven Dynamic Assortment in Online Platforms: Learning about Two Sides
affiliations: , University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill - Kenan-Flagler Business School and University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill - Operations Area

detail.title: Data-Driven Dynamic Assortment in Online Platforms: Learning about Two Sides
detail.abstract: We study a dynamic assortment problem on a two-sided service platform with incomplete information and heterogeneous customers in a discrete-time setting. In each period, a customer arrives seeking service, and the platform chooses an assortment of sellers to display. The customer then proposes a transaction to at most one seller in the assortment according to a multinomial logit choice model. After a fixed number of periods, sellers review the proposals they have received and each chooses at most one customer according to another multinomial logit choice model, after which the cycle repeats. A key challenge is that the platform does not know the choice-model parameters of either customers or sellers in advance. To our knowledge, this is the first study of a dynamic assortment problem in which both sides' choice parameters are unknown. We develop a data-driven algorithm that learns these parameters while optimizing the platform's objective over time. We evaluate performance using regret, which measures revenue loss relative to a clairvoyant benchmark that knows all parameters and customer arrivals in advance. We show that the algorithm's worst-case regret grows polylogarithmically over time, and we derive a matching lower bound, establishing its rate optimality.

title:
Pricing AI Software Services: 
Reallocating Value and Risk

detail.title:
Pricing AI Software Services: 
Reallocating Value and Risk

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is co-founder of CEADE Solutions, an agentic AI delivery firm. The frameworks in this paper draw on first-hand delivery experience at CEADE, which is disclosed in the paper as the source of the case study and worked examples.

detail.abstract:
This paper proposes a pricing framework for AI software services delivered using agentic AI.
Autonomous coding agents now do most of the implementation work that human engineers used
to charge for by the hour. Software services have been priced by the day for forty years on the
assumption that the cost of producing software scales with engineer time. Capable autonomous
coding agents have invalidated that assumption. The paper makes three arguments.

First, agentic software delivery splits the work into a 'thinking layer' (problem framing,
specification, scenario design, accountability) and a 'making layer' (implementation, testing,
refactoring), each with different unit economics and a different risk profile.

Second, the human role is diverging. Senior practitioners who can write a precise specification
are worth more than they were. Engineers doing mid-level implementation work are worth less.

Third, the price of frontier AI inference is not yet a stable market rate. Current per-token pricing
is a positioning bid by pre-IPO providers. Agencies building fixed-fee contracts against today's
subsidised rates are running a maturity-mismatch trade.

The paper proposes three pricing regimes: cost-decomposition, hybrid, and value-anchored
outcome-based pricing. It names several preconditions that must hold before value-anchored
pricing is achievable rather than aspirational. It sets out three contractual instruments that make
the framework operational: a minimum service standard, a measurement window, and a bilateral
repricing clause. It closes with a worked re-pricing of a real engagement in which a 2,500-hour
legacy quote was delivered using a near dark-factory pattern in 200 hours.

The paper is written for buyers of AI software services, principals at AI agencies and
consultancies pricing agentic delivery, as well as procurement leaders evaluating AI-led
professional services proposals

title:

Pricing AI Adoption in Public Real Estate

detail.title:
Talk is Cheap, Talent is Expensive: 
Pricing AI Adoption in Public Real Estate
detail.abstract: REITs are adopting AI across their core operations, but which AI disclosures do investors actually value? We classify AI language in REIT 10-K filings and earnings calls and test how markets price each type. Investors respond only to disclosure of internal operating use: it raises three-day earnings call returns by about 1 percentage point, while generic AI commentary draws no response. The reaction appears only for REITs that hired AI-skilled workers before the call, and general IT and analytics staffing produces no such effect, indicating that markets treat disclosure as credible only when costly, prior hiring backs it. These workforce-backed disclosures also predict subsequent gains in operating margins, the fundamentals on which REIT value rests. After ChatGPT's release, a long-short portfolio that buys REITs with pre-existing AI workforce and sells those without earns about 0.85% per month over 25 months. Talk is cheap; talent is what markets price.

title:
Need Engineering: 
Part C — The Ethics of Engineered Need

detail.title:
Need Engineering: 
Part C — The Ethics of Engineered Need

detail.abstract:
This paper presents Part C of the Need Engineering Framework — the ethical layer of a theoretical system that proposes human needs can be identified, activated, and expressed in novel behavioral forms through deliberate commercial design. The central question is: given that need formation can be made intentional, what obligations does that capacity create, and what happens commercially when those obligations are ignored?

The paper introduces the Ethics Tripartition — three categories of need engineering practice distinguished by their relationship to the human value they create or extract. Predatory need engineering builds dependency at human cost. Neutral need engineering creates habit without clear net benefit or harm. Regenerative need engineering builds dependency around genuine, compounding value. The paper argues that the distinction between these categories is not merely moral but commercially structural — predatory approaches destroy the resource that all commercial activity ultimately depends on.

Part C examines the mechanics of predatory need engineering — specifically the FOMO economy and dark pattern design — and argues that their short-term commercial effectiveness is inseparable from their long-term commercial fragility. It establishes the Regenerative Standard: five questions every practitioner should apply before scaling a product built on engineered need. The paper closes with a personal statement from the author on why the ethical layer was built into the Need Engineering Framework from its origin, rather than appended as a disclaimer after the commercial methodology was established.

title: Everything I Needed to Know to Fail in Life I Learned in College
affiliations: City University of New York (CUNY) - Koppelman School of Business and City University of New York (CUNY) - Paul H. Chook Department of Information Systems & Statistics

detail.title: Everything I Needed to Know to Fail in Life I Learned in College
detail.abstract: Higher education promises to develop critical thinkers, ethical leaders, and adaptable professionals. The evidence suggests it frequently does the opposite. This paper argues that universities are unintentionally cultivating habits of mind and institutional practices that set graduates up for failure, not despite their degrees, but partly because of them. Drawing on research across management, psychology, organizational behavior, and education, we examine how institutions neglect the competencies society most urgently needs: intellectual humility, active listening, ethical reasoning, constructive disagreement, adaptability, and strength of character. These deficits are compounded by grade inflation, academic dishonesty, and ideological conformity, including narrow institutional conceptions of diversity that fixate on race and gender while ignoring equally consequential forms of bias based on class, disability, political affiliation, geographic origin, and educational status. Crucially, this perspective views higher education as fully redeemable. Because these essential competencies represent learnable skills instead of fixed traits, universities remain the ideal vehicles for their cultivation, provided they find the institutional will to change. The gap between what colleges claim to produce and what employers and society actually receive can be prevented. It is a choice, and it can be reversed.

title: How Would Monopsony Employer Hurt Labor? A Simple Dynamic Model

detail.abstract: Recently, a debate has emerged about the growing market power of large firms and its implications for labor markets. Our simple model shows that monopsony employers tend to hire fewer workers and set wages below the socially optimal level, generating what we call incentive-driven unemployment. Although this structure encourages workers to exert effort, it also compresses wages, producing substantially smaller wage differentials among workers-both within and across firms-than would reflect their productivity differences. In equilibrium, income inequality is excessive, labor is misallocated, and the job-finding rate is notably lower than the social optimum. Our numerical examples demonstrate the economic importance of these effects and illustrate realistic labor-market dynamics and plausible micro wage-productivity elasticities.
