detail.abstract: EU antitrust is at the crossroads. It faces calls to be more supportive of corporate sustainability initiatives and, since the publication of the Draghi Report, increased pressure not to stand in the way of the global competitiveness of European industries. This article develops a pragmatic plan to reap the full environmental potential of EU competition policy. It draws attention to the instrumental and institutional constraints encountered when actively pursuing sustainability through antitrust. Relying on the theory of economic policy and from a pro-enforcement standpoint, the article ponders how the instruments and principles devised in the ongoing antitrust reform may be used to encourage sustainable technology and, in turn, boost growth. The aim is to find a path towards an eco-friendly yet effective competition policy.

title: Marketing World Models
affiliations: Monash University - Department of Marketing and University of Melbourne

detail.title: Marketing World Models
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence has evolved from prediction and content generation to the simulation of entire environments. We introduce Marketing World Models (MWMs) as a new class of AI systems that are deployed through varying levels of environmental realism and agent autonomy to model and simulate customer behavior, firm strategies, and market evolution within synthetic marketing ecosystems. Drawing on strategic marketing capabilities frameworks, we explain how MWM represents a capacity enabler that empowers dynamic, architectural, cross-functional, and specialized marketing capabilities through synthetic agency and scalable counterfactuals. We then identify the foundational and design elements of MWMs, providing definitional clarity and grounding each element to current managerial use cases. Next, we provide a typology of MWMs based on a 2 × 2 matrix that crosses environmental realism and agent autonomy, elucidating the different manifestations of these AI ecosystems (LL: diagnostic sandboxes, LH: agentic decision engines, HL: world dreamers, HH: synthetic market ecosystems) and how they are suited to address different marketing problems. We conclude by providing an integrative framework of MWMs with testable propositions. Our work provides a marketing-specific foundation to deploy MWMs as strategic capability and explains how, under what conditions, and for what common marketing problems do world models create value for firms.

title: Cross-border Consumer Protection
affiliations: Humboldt University of Berlin

detail.title: Cross-border Consumer Protection

contentType.other: forthcoming in Handbook European Consumer Law (edited by Christoph Busch and Christian Twigg-Flessner)

detail.abstract:
Cross-border consumer transactions are essential to the functioning of the European Single Market. Yet, despite decades of European integration, consumers and businesses continue to face legal uncertainty arising from the coexistence of multiple national legal systems. Uncertainty regarding the applicable law, jurisdiction, and the enforcement of rights may discourage cross-border contracting and thereby undermine the economic benefits of market integration.

This chapter examines the legal framework that the European Union has developed to address these challenges and to promote consumer confidence in cross-border transactions. It analyses four key dimensions of European consumer protection: the determination of the applicable law, jurisdictional rules, mechanisms for the cross-border enforcement of claims, and alternative dispute resolution. Particular attention is paid to the consumer-protective architecture of the Rome I Regulation and the Brussels Ia Regulation, as well as to European instruments such as the European Small Claims Procedure, the European Payment Order Procedure, and the Consumer ADR framework.

The chapter argues that European law grants consumers a series of far-reaching privileges, notably access to the law and courts of their home state and simplified mechanisms for the enforcement and settlement of claims. These measures have significantly reduced some of the legal barriers traditionally associated with cross-border consumer contracts. However, empirical evidence suggests that consumer trust in cross-border trade remains limited. The chapter identifies several reasons for this outcome, including regulatory complexity, inconsistencies between different legal instruments, limited awareness of existing rights and remedies, and the practical shortcomings of enforcement mechanisms.

It concludes that while the European Union has made substantial progress in facilitating cross-border consumer contracting, further reforms - particularly in the areas of simplification, digitalisation, and the balancing of consumer and business interests - are necessary to realize the full potential of the European Single Market.

title: Cognitive Amplification Inequality Theory (CAIT): A Structural Production Framework for AI Integrated Economies

detail.title: Cognitive Amplification Inequality Theory (CAIT): A Structural Production Framework for AI Integrated Economies
detail.abstract:
This paper is written in a two layer format consisting of a managerial layer and a technical layer. The managerial layer emphasizes strategic interpretation and organizational value, while the technical layer focuses on formal procedures, mathematical structure, and operator level rigor. Cognitive Amplification Inequality Theory (CAIT) formalizes how economically relevant intelligence is transformed under LLM mediated augmentation. The theory introduces a multiplicative production operator 
AP = C × A,
where C denotes intrinsic cognition and A denotes AI amplification capacity. It demonstrates that amplification induces nonlinear productivity gains and structurally increases dispersion, satisfying 
Var(C × A) > Var(C). 
CAIT frames AI integrated economies as socio-cognitive systems in which productivity, inequality, and occupational structure emerge from heterogeneous access to and integration with amplification systems. The framework provides a unified basis for analyzing cognitive underutilization, AI adoption gaps, and amplification driven divergence in modern economies.

title: Essays in Personnel Economics: Aging Workforce and Worker Substitutability

detail.title: Essays in Personnel Economics: Aging Workforce and Worker Substitutability
detail.abstract: This dissertation studies how retirement age reforms reshape labor markets beyond individual retirement decisions, focusing on firms, coworkers, and workplace interactions. Using quasi-experimental evidence from German pension reforms that raised women’s early retirement age, I examine how delayed retirements affect internal labor markets, worker substitutability, and peer behavior at older ages. The first chapter shows that retaining older workers generates substantial intra-firm spillovers. Delayed retirements reduce internal promotions and external hiring of younger coworkers, with the largest losses among middle-aged workers closest to older workers on career ladders. These effects are highly structured: promotion crowd-out arises in dense internal labor markets with intense competition and operates primarily within jobcells, while coworkers in other jobcells can benefit when retained older workers possess firm-specific human capital. Hiring declines, by contrast, are concentrated in thin external labor markets where replacement is difficult, highlighting that without accounting for hiring frictions, crowd-out effects cannot be interpreted as pure measures of worker substitutability. The second chapter demonstrates that retirement age reforms help firms retain less substitutable workers with job-specific skills and managerial responsibilities, preserving valuable human capital that would otherwise be lost through voluntary exits. The third chapter shows that reform effects are further amplified through peer behavior: women are more likely to remain employed at older ages when their coworkers do so, explained by conformity, information, and work complementarity mechanisms. Together, these chapters show the interdependence of coworker careers through slot constraints, human capital, and social interactions.

title: Culture, Religion, and Women Entrepreneurs' Financial Well-being and Quality of Life: Evidence from SMEs in Southeast Asia
affiliations: University of Economics Ho Chi Minh City and

detail.title: Culture, Religion, and Women Entrepreneurs' Financial Well-being and Quality of Life: Evidence from SMEs in Southeast Asia
detail.abstract: Access to credit is a foundational determinant of women entrepreneurs' financial well-being, economic autonomy, and quality of life, yet its drivers remain poorly understood beyond firmlevel characteristics. Existing research has largely overlooked how cultural context and religious diversity shape gendered financial access and its implications for well-being. This study combines World Bank Enterprise Surveys (WBES) with World Happiness Report (WHR) data and applies the Culture-Based Development (CBD) framework, capturing Cultural Heritage (CH) and Living Culture (LC), within a logistic regression model with interaction effects in Southeast Asia. The results reveal a context-dependent female advantage in credit access, where Living Culture acts as a gender-equalizing mechanism that reduces financial constraints, particularly in Buddhist-majority contexts. These findings offer actionable insights for designing culturally sensitive financial inclusion policies that can meaningfully improve women's economic well-being across diverse Southeast Asian societies.

title: Distribution Mechanisms and Conditional Aggregate Effects in Interprovincial Price Differentials: Evidence from a Penn-Balassa-Samuelson Framework in China

detail.title: Distribution Mechanisms and Conditional Aggregate Effects in Interprovincial Price Differentials: Evidence from a Penn-Balassa-Samuelson Framework in China
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the mechanisms behind interprovincial price differentials in China by extending the Penn-Balassa-Samuelson (PBS) framework with distribution costs and conditional aggregate effects. Theoretical analysis shows that local non-tradable inputs embedded in retail tradable prices (e.g., transportation, warehousing, and retail services) generate systematic deviations from the law of one price at the interprovincial level. It further implies that the effect of relative tradable-sector productivity on the aggregate price level is conditional rather than universally positive. Using provincial panel data, the empirical strategy proceeds in three steps: identifying the core productivity channel, decomposing LOP deviations and relative-price components, and estimating conditional aggregate effects through state-dependent specifications. The results show that distribution-related mechanisms significantly account for interprovincial retail-price deviations; the positive effect of tradable-sector relative productivity on sectoral relative prices is robust; and the impact on aggregate prices is strongly state-dependent, becoming weak or even negative under certain structural conditions. The paper thus unifies LOP deviations and unstable aggregate-price effects within one structural framework and provides an integrated theory-to-evidence explanation for domestic price dispersion.

title: Administrative Organization of Ismail County in the Composition of Lower Danube Land (1938-1940)
affiliations: "Dunarea de Jos" University of Galati

detail.title: Administrative Organization of Ismail County in the Composition of Lower Danube Land (1938-1940)
detail.abstract: Relevance. The study of the 1938-1940 period in the history of Ismail County provides relevant insights into the evolution of territorial organization in the interwar Romanian space and contributes to understanding the relationship between administrative centralization, regionalization, and the functionality of local administrative structures. The purpose of the study is to examine the specific features of a territorial reorganization model dominated by administrative centralization, using Ismail County as a case study. Results. The experience of administrative reorganization in Romania during the period 1938-1940 elucidates the limitations of a centralized model of administrative regionalization. In the case of Ismail County, administrative reorganization overlapped with major political and territorial transformations that affected the county's institutional stability. Examining the case of Ismail County within the Lower Danube Land provides insight into the practical implementation of this reform, the principles guiding territorial delimitation, and the functioning of local administration during a short but significant episode in Romania's administrative history. Conclusions. The subnational administrative system established by the Administrative Law of 1938 reinforced the centralizing tendencies of the state and reduced the autonomy that counties had previously exercised in managing local affairs. At the same time, the reform introduced several key principles for territorial organization, such as the economic viability of administrative divisions, the accessibility of transport routes, and the cohesion of local communities. Although the regional structure of the Lands existed only for a short period, these principles continue to hold relevance in contemporary debates on administrative-territorial reform. The case of Ismail County thus highlights both the objectives and the constraints of administrative modernization pursued under Romania's interwar authoritarian regime.

title: Perception-driven Inflation Persistence: A DSGE Model with Diagnostic Expectations and Policy Implications
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Perception-driven Inflation Persistence: A DSGE Model with Diagnostic Expectations and Policy Implications
detail.abstract: This paper examines why disinflation in Poland remained slow and persistent following the 2021-2022 energy price shock, despite a rapid decline in headline inflation. It evaluates whether systematic misperceptions of inflation contribute to this persistence and explores the corresponding implications for monetary policy. To address this question, a New Keynesian DSGE model with a perception channel is developed. A fraction of firms forms expectations using households' perceived inflation, generating a propagation mechanism driven by diagnostic expectations and backward-looking information. Perceived inflation is modeled as a predetermined process, allowing it to influence inflation dynamics without assuming strict exogeneity. The model is estimated for Poland using the Simulated Method of Moments on quarterly data for 2010-2024. The perception parameter is positive and statistically significant (δ = 0.14), with identification supported by moment sensitivity and robustness diagnostics. The perception channel becomes economically relevant primarily during the post-2020 highinflation period, when perception-driven dynamics amplify peak inflation and contribute to a more gradual disinflation process. Impulse responses show stronger and more persistent inflation, while variance decomposition suggests that perception shocks account for around 20% of inflation variability. A one-standard-deviation perception shock increases inflation by approximately 0.3 percentage points, with effects that accumulate over time. From a policy perspective, an augmented Taylor rule that responds to the perception gap improves stabilization performance. The loss-minimizing specification assigns a moderate weight to this variable (φ_p* ≈ 0.4), implying that policy should react more strongly when perceived inflation deviates from actual outcomes. At the same time, the effectiveness of this response is statedependent, calling for cautious and context-specific implementation. Overall, the findings highlight that distorted perceptions can act as an endogenous source of inflation persistence and that incorporating perception dynamics can improve both model performance and policy design.

title: Can soft-policy interventions address motoring harms? A randomized controlled trial of safety warnings on Sports Utility Vehicle (SUV) adverts
affiliations: Swansea University, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Swansea University

detail.title: Can soft-policy interventions address motoring harms? A randomized controlled trial of safety warnings on Sports Utility Vehicle (SUV) adverts
detail.abstract: Larger vehicles like SUVs and pickup trucks impose elevated risks onto other road users, but we do not know whether making this salient to the public might shift their choices toward safer vehicles. We conducted a randomized controlled trial with a demographically stratified sample of 2105 UK residents. People viewed mockup SUV advertisements with or without information overlays indicating the greater risks these vehicles create for pedestrians and cyclists. Interest in purchasing an SUV and perceived risks were assessed before and after viewing the advertisements. Overall, participants who initially did not agree that SUVs present greater danger to vulnerable road users were 28.2% more likely to do so after seeing the warning message compared to controls, though the effect was smaller among current SUV owners and those interested in buying one. There was relatively little change in future SUV purchase intentions after viewing the warning information, even among drivers who recognised SUVs were more dangerous and even among drivers who claimed other people’s safety was important when choosing a vehicle. This suggests that warning messages are unlikely to influence many consumers toward safer vehicles. Building on earlier car-buying research, we suggest many people’s decision processes might not involve a stage in which they narrow down potential vehicles based on pro-social information. More widely, drawing on other transportation research, we argue that thanks to entrenched socio-cultural norms – in this case, of tolerating avoidable motoring harms – information-based interventions are unlikely substantially to change any road transportation behaviours, and that hard-policy actions will usually be necessary.

title: Contextualised Transformational Leadership and Institutional Reform in Selected African Public Agencies: A Systematised Narrative Review

detail.title: Contextualised Transformational Leadership and Institutional Reform in Selected African Public Agencies: A Systematised Narrative Review
detail.abstract: This article examines transformational leadership as a possible contributor to institutional reform in selected African public agencies. It argues that transformational leadership cannot be treated as a portable managerial technique that automatically improves public administration. In African public-sector settings, leadership effects are shaped by institutional capacity, political incentives, ethical credibility, administrative traditions, citizen trust, and socio-cultural expectations about collective responsibility. Using a systematised narrative review and doctrinal-policy synthesis, the article brings together leadership theory, African public administration literature, governance datasets and selected country examples from Rwanda, South Africa, Kenya, Ghana and Nigeria. The paper develops a Contextualised Transformational Leadership for African Public Agencies (CTL-APA) framework. The framework identifies five conditions under which transformational leadership behaviours are most likely to support reform: ethical credibility, Ubuntu-informed collective purpose, institutional capacity building, accountability architecture and adaptive service innovation. Current governance evidence is used cautiously. The 2024 Ibrahim Index of African Governance reports that overall governance progress in Africa stalled in 2022 after a period of near stagnation, while Afrobarometer evidence shows declining citizen trust in several public institutions across surveyed countries. These patterns support the article's central argument that leadership reform must be connected to institutional legitimacy rather than framed only as individual charisma. The article concludes that transformational leadership may support reform where leaders are ethically credible, institutionally constrained, administratively capable and embedded in systems of citizen accountability. Where these conditions are absent, transformational language can become symbolic, personalistic or even pseudo-transformational. The contribution of the article is therefore not a claim that transformational leadership is a universal remedy, but a safer framework for adapting it to African public agencies in ways that are culturally grounded, institutionally realistic and evidence-aware.

title: Geopolitical Distance and the Sensitivity of Bilateral Capital Flows to Global Risk

detail.title: Geopolitical Distance and the Sensitivity of Bilateral Capital Flows to Global Risk
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether bilateral geopolitical distance (GPD) modulates portfolio capital flow sensitivity to global risk. Extending Albuquerque (2003)'s model of cross-border capital flows under expropriation risk from imperfect contract enforcement, I argue that more geopolitically distant country pairs face tighter participation constraints, attenuating their responsiveness to global volatility. Estimating a gravity model with origin-time and destination-time fixed effects on a 2001-2018 panel of bilateral portfolio flows, using UNGA voting divergence as a GPD proxy, is consistent with this prediction. Higher GPD significantly reduces flow sensitivity to VIX movements and increases the FDI-to-portfolio-investment ratio. These findings demonstrate that geopolitical alignment shapes both the level and the risk-transmission capacity of cross-border financial linkages.

title: Machines Against Workers? The Heterogeneous Impact of Robots on Union Strength
affiliations: and Duke University - Department of Political Science

detail.title: Machines Against Workers? The Heterogeneous Impact of Robots on Union Strength
detail.abstract: Does the increasing automation of the workplace weaken labor unions? The dominant hypothesis in current political economy research is that automation weakens unions and, as a result, undermines worker voice in democratic politics. However, the standard economic theory of automation does not consider unions, and recent political science studies focus on estimating average effects. We argue that the relationship between automation and organized labor is heterogeneous. We integrate task-based automation into a model of strategic worker mobilization and collective bargaining. Our new model suggests that automation can disempower but also empower unions. Empirically, we use quantile instrumental variable regression and find that the impact of robotization on unionization significantly varies across regional labor markets in the US. Consistent with the theoretical perspective, this heterogeneity is mostly due to unobserved characteristics. Our results suggest that research on the political economy impacts of automation should pay more attention to strategic worker mobilization.

title: The Fiscal Consequences of Prolonged High Interest Rates: A Cross-Country Analysis of Debt-Interest Spirals
affiliations: Columbia University

detail.title: The Fiscal Consequences of Prolonged High Interest Rates: A Cross-Country Analysis of Debt-Interest Spirals
detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether persistent increases in the effective interest rate on government debt trigger non-linear, explosive debt dynamics in advanced economies. Using an annual panel of 34 advanced economies from 2004 to 2025, we employ panel local projections (Jordà, 2005) and Hansen (1999) threshold estimation. A one-percentage-point increase in the effective interest rate raises the debt-to-GDP ratio by 11.1 percentage points after three years in countries with initial debt above 90 % of GDP (p = 0.008), with no significant effect below that threshold. Hansen threshold estimation identifies two breakpoints: 70.7 % and 112.7 % of GDP, with the snowball coefficient rising from 0.20 to 0.97 to 1.47 across regimes (p = 0.004 for the second threshold). A Bohn (1998) fiscal reaction function shows a positive fiscal response to lagged debt (coefficient 0.033, p = 0.002) when the interest-rate-growth differential is negative, but the response halves and becomes insignificant when r > g (interaction-0.0145, p = 0.007). These results are consistent with a non-linear debt-interest spiral, with a critical danger zone above 90 % of GDP. Policy implications include state-contingent fiscal rules and recognition that monetary tightening imposes binding fiscal constraints in highly indebted economies.

detail.abstract: The WTO's most-favored nation treatment (MFN) principle aimed at preventing discriminatory practices was developed in an era of deepening convergence between trading partners. The violation of the MFN became a symbol of global trade policy in 2025. The tariff «power-play» of the acting US administration as well as other countries' retaliatory measures sparked substantive discussions about the future of the MFN principle in the WTO. The need to rethink the functioning of one of the basic principles of world trade has been raised by many participants of the multilateral trading system.

title: Revisiting the Effects of Fiscal Policy in the Modified New Keynesian Model
affiliations: The Japan Research Institute, Limited

detail.title: Revisiting the Effects of Fiscal Policy in the Modified New Keynesian Model
detail.abstract: This paper modifies the New Keynesian (NK) model by incorporating two realistic assumptions. The first is a monetary policy rule that allows for cases where the Taylor Principle is not satisfied. The second is the treatment of the consolidated government's budget equation not as a "constraint" as assumed in standard economics, but as an accounting "identity," with increases in government spending financed by increases in the money stock. Furthermore, by interpreting the state of reaching "potential GDP" as the state in which the economy's real resource limit has been reached, and combining this with the government budget identity, the model incorporates the ideas of Modern Monetary Theory (MMT) into the NK model. Using this model, we show that when actual GDP is below potential GDP, an increase in government spending raises private consumption and increases household utility (the multiplier effect). We also show that once the economy reaches potential GDP, further government spending depresses consumption and raises the inflation rate; however, if government spending expands potential GDP itself through infrastructure maintenance, R&D, and education investment, further welfare improvements are possible.

detail.abstract: We study the rise of nonbank financial intermediation and its implications for systemic risk. We develop a structural network model of banks and nonbank financial institutions (NBFIs) that decomposes intermediation into a capacity channel, driven by bank balance-sheet constraints, and a reliance channel, reflecting NBFI funding reliance. Using U.S. banking confidential supervisory data, we estimate key structural parameters and quantify both channels. We find that fluctuations in bank-NBFI intermediation are primarily explained by the reliance channel, with variation in NBFI fragility emerging as the dominant driver. We show that NBFI intermediation can amplify shocks through funding interconnectedness.

title: Cross-Sectional Return Prediction in Cryptocurrency Markets Using Variational Latent Factor Models
affiliations: UC Berkeley

detail.title: Cross-Sectional Return Prediction in Cryptocurrency Markets Using Variational Latent Factor Models
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the application of variational autoencoder-based latent factor models to cryptocurrency markets. We adapt the FactorVAE architecture, originally designed for equity markets, to a universe of 50 major cryptocurrencies using technical indicators derived from price and volume data. Our empirical analysis covers the period 2019-2024, with out-of-sample testing in 2024. We implement and compare seven distinct trading strategies exploiting the model's cross-sectional predictions, including directional, market-neutral, volatility-adjusted, and momentum-filtered approaches. Results demonstrate that the model generates economically significant signals, with six out of seven strategies achieving positive Sharpe ratios exceeding 1.0. The Momentum Filter strategy emerges as the most effective approach, achieving a 269.8% return with a Sharpe ratio of 2.12. We further examine latent factor stabilization techniques and find that temporal regularization produces more interpretable factor dynamics without sacrificing predictive accuracy. These findings suggest that deep generative models offer promising tools for understanding and exploiting cross-sectional structure in cryptocurrency markets.

title: Community Willingness to Pay for Biodiversity Conservation in Old Oyo National Park, Nigeria
affiliations: Federal University of Technology, Akure and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Community Willingness to Pay for Biodiversity Conservation in Old Oyo National Park, Nigeria
detail.abstract: Biodiversity and ecosystem services play a critical role in supporting livelihoods, environmental sustainability, and socioeconomic development, particularly in developing countries where communities depend heavily on natural resources. This study assessed the economic valuation of ecosystem services and community willingness to pay (WTP) for biodiversity conservation in Old Oyo National Park, Nigeria. Specifically, the study identified the major ecosystem services within the park, examined community support for conservation initiatives, evaluated local perceptions of ecosystem services, and estimated the value attached to biodiversity conservation by support-zone communities. A multi-stage sampling technique was adopted to select respondents from communities bordering the park, and 384 structured questionnaires were administered. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, Chi-square analysis, and Analysis of Variance (ANOVA), while the Contingent Valuation Method (CVM) was used to estimate respondents' willingness to pay for conservation. Findings revealed that the park provides important ecosystem services including fertile land, medicinal plants, fauna resources, clean water, and cultural values. The study further showed that 88.8% of respondents supported biodiversity conservation, while 67.4% expressed willingness to contribute financially toward conservation initiatives. Socioeconomic characteristics, environmental perception, and perceived benefits from the park significantly influenced conservation support and willingness to pay. The study concludes that ecosystem services from Old Oyo National Park provide substantial socioeconomic and environmental benefits to adjoining communities. Therefore, integrating local communities into conservation planning, improving environmental awareness, and establishing sustainable conservation financing mechanisms are essential for long-term biodiversity protection and ecosystem sustainability in Nigeria.

title: Climate Action through Financial Inclusion: The Role of DCGF in Fostering Eco-Friendly Enterprises

detail.title: Climate Action through Financial Inclusion: The Role of DCGF in Fostering Eco-Friendly Enterprises
detail.abstract: Nepal ranks among the ten most climate-vulnerable countries in the world yet contributes less than 0.02% of global greenhouse gas emissions, and faces a USD 3.6 billion financing gap for the small and medium enterprises (SMEs) that anchor its non-agricultural economy. This paper investigates how Nepal's Deposit and Credit Guarantee Fund (DCGF) can leverage a dedicated green guarantee scheme to simultaneously advance climate action and financial inclusion for eco-friendly SMEs, in alignment with the country's 2045 net-zero target. Grounded in information asymmetry theory and a dual market failure framework, the paper combines structured comparative analysis of green credit guarantee schemes across six emerging and developing economies (India, Kenya, Cambodia, Ghana, Bangladesh, Indonesia), institutional mapping of Nepal's evolving green finance architecture including the 2024 Nepal Green Finance Taxonomy and the World Bank's USD 95 million Sustainable and Inclusive Finance Project (2026), and a leverage and fiscal-exposure sensitivity analysis based on the Udaya Guarantee Fund pilot in Koshi Province. The analysis shows that DCGF's current SME guarantee scheme is sector-focused and has a green gap. The Udaya Fund's projected 13:1 leverage ratio suggests that under conservative claim assumptions a USD 10-15 million capital could expand USD 130-200 million in new SME lending to sectors of clean energy, waste management and circular economic activities. Key constraints include lender capacity to analyse green sectors, absence of green eligibility standards or green tagging in DCGF's mandates, and fiscal exposure risks at high leverage. This paper presents six parameters for national green SME guarantee scheme operation and contributes to the literature on green finance in climate-vulnerable emerging economies.

title: Do Export Bans Reshape Food Trade? Evidence from India’s Rice Exports to Sub-Saharan Africa

detail.title: Do Export Bans Reshape Food Trade? Evidence from India’s Rice Exports to Sub-Saharan Africa
detail.abstract: This paper asks whether India’s removal of its non-basmati rice export ban in September 2011 produced a persistent reallocation of trade toward Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), and whether that shift was supply-driven rather than the result of a contemporaneous African demand shock. Using UN Comtrade bilateral trade data for 1996–2024 (12,303 exporter–destination–year observations), we combine a triple-difference (DDD) design, exporter-specific trend-break models, log-ratio regressions, and dynamic event-study specifications. Four hypotheses are tested: (H1) India’s share of exports to SSA rises after 2011 beyond global export recovery; (H2) incumbent exporters lose relative market share in African destinations; (H3) the shift persists over the following decade rather than reverting; and (H4) aggregate African rice demand shows no discrete structural break coinciding with liberalisation. The core DDD coefficient on the India × SSA × Post interaction is 0.176 in the market-share specification (robust p < 0.001) and 1.441 in the log-value specification (robust p < 0.001), implying that India’s export value to SSA after 2011 is approximately exp(1.441) ≈ 4.2 times larger than exporter and destination trends alone predict. Log-ratio regressions indicate that India’s export value became approximately 22 times larger relative to Thailand, 30 times larger relative to Vietnam, and 14 times larger relative to Pakistan. India’s average SSA quantity share rose from 35.4 per cent in the pre-ban period to 24.5 per cent during the ban and to 59.3 per cent post-liberalisation. Aggregate African imports display no positive structural break in 2011. The evidence is consistent with a durable, supply-driven reconfiguration of trade following India’s re-entry into a thin global rice market.

title: Mechanisms of Learning in Collaborative Jobs *
affiliations: Central European University and Corvinus University of Budapest

detail.title: Mechanisms of Learning in Collaborative Jobs *
detail.abstract: We investigate mechanisms of learning in collaborative environments using granular data from European men's football, overcoming limitations of linked employer-employee data. First, conditional on average quality, team composition and exposure to stars are not associated with learning. Second, peer quality is associated with reduced task allocation, leading standard approaches to underestimate learning effects by approximately 30%. Third, intensive collaboration with high-quality peers predicts stronger learning gains. Fourth, peer effects manifest in learnable skills (passing) but not in innate abilities (speed), providing evidence against selection bias. Finally, learning persists after job changes, suggesting genuine human capital accumulation rather than temporary complementarities.

title: A Mechanism for Outcome Markets: Parimutuel Derivatives with Temporal Commitment Pricing

detail.title: A Mechanism for Outcome Markets: Parimutuel Derivatives with Temporal Commitment Pricing

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has no financial conflicts of interest related to this work.

detail.abstract: Existing prediction-market designs bundle three functions — aggregate belief estimation, entry pricing, and liquidity provision — into a single market price. We identify a class of events for which this bundling appears structurally unnecessary: events with a liquid observable underlying from which probability can be inferred exogenously. For such events, the relevant design question is no longer how to discover probability through trading, but how to distribute speculative surplus once that probability is exogenously given. We articulate one realisation of this unbundling — a class of parimutuel derivatives with payoff-side temporal commitment pricing — and test it against three baselines (plain parimutuel, CPMM, LMSR) on 20,000 event windows drawn from real cryptocurrency price data (≈80,000 event-simulations across mechanisms), complemented by a counterfactual replay across 12 settled Polymarket binary markets (581,960 trades, $117.5M total stake). The proposed mechanism redistributes toward earlier commitments in 11 of 12 markets, with trades placed correctly in the first 30% of the event window earning approximately 2.1 times their plain-parimutuel counterfactual. An ablation shows the time factor drives the redistribution while the probability factor halves the cost borne by late-informed traders; a calibration test finds the market price retains incremental information beyond our observation-derived signal, so the redundancy premise holds only to first order. We characterise the mechanism's failure surface via a pool-size sweep (25–500 agents) and an adversarial battery covering volatility manipulation and oracle staleness. The unbundling reframing — separating belief aggregation from settlement architecture — is the broader conceptual contribution; the specific mechanism is one implementation.

title: What Do AI Companies Deserve?  Shapley Attribution and Optimal Tax Theory

detail.title: What Do AI Companies Deserve?  Shapley Attribution and Optimal Tax Theory
detail.abstract: Should artificial intelligence (AI) companies be taxed, and if so, how?  This paper presents two arguments which together support an ability-indexed tax on AI systems.  First: AI companies--including frontier labs and traditional firms using AI in production--do not deserve all of their income.  Because AI companies do not contribute important elements of their models, including (in part) their algorithms and the public data on which they were trained, on a desert-based normative framework they have limited moral entitlement to their income.  I formally decompose AI models using the game-theoretic concept of Shapley value, showing that the general point about limited AI company deserts is robust.  Indeed, the deserved income is plausibly small.  Second, I turn to the public finance question of how the excess income can be efficiently redistributed.  Drawing on optimal tax theory, I present a model in which an ability-indexed AI tax avoids the intensive margin distortion familiar from human taxation.  This is because AI relaxes a key constraint of optimal tax theory: Unlike humans, it is possible to observe AI system ability.  Another ramification of the model is that relatively high-ability/high-profit AI systems will be taxed down to a common level of profit.  If individuals, firms, and others ought to get what they deserve, there is a strong moral case for taxing AI companies, and good theoretical grounds to believe the revenue generated can be redistributed efficiently.

title: The Compressed Economic Integration Framework (CEI)

detail.title: The Compressed Economic Integration Framework (CEI)

detail.abstract: The Compressed Economic Integration (CEI) Framework is an original conceptual model that explains a specific and undertheorized mechanism of aging immigrant retirement vulnerability in the United States. While existing frameworks — notably the Latent Cumulative Disadvantage (LCD) model and the emerging migrant pension penalty literature — document that immigrants face lower retirement income than native-born workers across the life course, neither framework adequately addresses the situation of late-arrival immigrants who enter the United States during midlife. The CEI Framework proposes that late-arrival immigrants face not merely accumulated disadvantages, but a structurally compressed and architecturally misaligned integration timeline. U.S. retirement systems — including Social Security, employer-sponsored 401(k) plans, and ERISA-protected pensions — were designed with the assumption of a full-career domestic worker: someone who begins contributing to retirement systems in their twenties and accumulates forty or more years of credit before retiring. Late-arrival immigrants, typically entering after age 40, cannot replicate this trajectory regardless of their work ethic, income level, or legal status. This paper formally introduces the CEI Framework through three defining dimensions: (1) Temporal Compression — the shortened accumulation window that falls below the viable thresholds embedded in retirement system design; (2) Structural Displacement — the systematic misalignment between retirement system eligibility rules and the non-linear employment trajectories of late-arrival immigrants; and (3) Compounding Vulnerability — the interactive amplification of temporal and structural barriers by classification exclusion, low wages, language barriers, and transnational family obligations. Four testable propositions are derived from the framework to guide future empirical research. The paper concludes by differentiating CEI from the LCD Framework and the migrant pension penalty model, and by identifying policy and research implications.

detail.abstract: The emergence of AI assistants and agents is transforming market dynamics, favouring a shift in competition away from individual products and towards integrated services, and from competition between firms to competition between ecosystems. This transition is reshaping power relations along the vertical chain; On the one hand, vertically integrated providers may deploy leveraging strategies to favour their own AI tools, and may further use these tools to extract rents from downstream intermediaries. On the other hand, the success of agentic AI and the proliferation of strategic collaborations may facilitate entry, offer new paths to market, and possibly challenge the hegemony of the established ecosystem. This paper explores these developments and the relationship between intra-ecosystem competition and inter-AI (ecosystem) competition. In doing so, it reflects on the emergence of frenemy relationship between market players, and the adequacy of current competition law analysis in evaluating complex inter-and intra AI competition.

title: Measuring Investor Disagreement: Proxies, Pitfalls, and a Path Forward
affiliations: Auburn University - Harbert College of Business, Duke University - Fuqua School of Business and University of Lausanne - Faculty of Business and Economics (HEC Lausanne)

detail.title: Measuring Investor Disagreement: Proxies, Pitfalls, and a Path Forward
detail.abstract: Disagreement among investors is central to modern theories of trading and asset prices, yet it is fundamentally unobservable. We review the empirical literature that measures it, which now spans dozens of proxies drawn from analyst forecasts, return volatility, trading and short interest, institutional holdings, option prices, and, more recently, text and machine learning methods. We organize this literature around the constructs these proxies are meant to capture, their data requirements, and the alternative interpretations that limit each one. A recurring theme is that the leading proxies are only weakly correlated with one another in the cross section of firms, so empirical conclusions about disagreement can depend heavily on which proxy is used. We discuss why this pattern arises, survey recent efforts to combine proxies and to discipline the choice among them and offer practical guidance for researchers who measure disagreement or who must assess findings that rest on a particular proxy.

title: Spatial misallocation and welfare effects of government subsidy: Evidence from China’s new energy vehicle industry
affiliations: Hunan University, Nankai University and Hunan University

detail.title: Spatial misallocation and welfare effects of government subsidy: Evidence from China’s new energy vehicle industry
detail.abstract: This paper combines a multi-sector spatial equilibrium model and generalized difference-in-differences design to evaluate China’s New Energy Vehicle (NEV) pilot program over 2009–2022, under which 88 prefecture-level cities were sequentially designated as eligible for production and consumption subsidies. Results robustly show that NEV pilot designation raises NEV output by 31% and battery-cell capacity by 35%, with no detectable substitution away from internal-combustion-engine production. We embed the same data in a four-sector spatial model in the Caliendo-Parro (2015) tradition with mobile labor, monopolistic competition, sector-specific agglomeration, and prefecture-level input-output linkages calibrated from the 2017 China Multi-Regional Input-Output Table. Removing the subsidies in the calibrated 2022 equilibrium lowers aggregate real income by 0.42% gross, or 0.34% net of the marginal cost of public funds, and lowers NEV-sector real output by 13.6%; roughly 71% of the gain is captured by pilot prefectures and 29% propagates through input-output linkages to non-pilot prefectures. A misallocation analysis indicates that an alternative subsidy schedule re-weighted in proportion to the recovered fundamental productivity in the NEV powertrain sector would deliver a 24% larger welfare gain at the same fiscal cost. The cost-benefit ratio of the program, excluding unmeasured environmental externalities, is 1.18.

title: The Camouflage Of Expertise: The Failed Promise Of Ftc Independence
affiliations: William & Mary Law School

detail.title: The Camouflage Of Expertise: The Failed Promise Of Ftc Independence
detail.abstract:
This article critiques the claim that independence promotes FTC expertise, using the Commission’s 2024 ban of employee noncompete agreements (“NCAs”) as a case study.  President Biden urged the Commission to "curtail” NCAs, claiming that employers use growing labor market power to impose them.  President Biden’s three Commission appointees—including the two removed commissioners—approved the ban, which President Biden endorsed.

The article shows that the process resulting in the ban ignored procedural norms designed to ensure that commissioners gather and consider data and expertise external to the Agency.  The Rule ignored or mischaracterized record evidence contradicting key empirical assumptions supporting the ban.  The Rule also repeatedly ignored comments on the proposal highlighting such evidence or refuting assumptions informing the ban. 

The refusal to consider data and significant comments violated the APA’s requirement that commissioners “consider relevant material” submitted in response to proposed rules.  Such refusal also rendered the resulting rule arbitrary and capricious, because the Commission did not “consider the relevant factors” when assessing the proposal and suggested alternatives.  Despite their self-portrayal as independent experts, the removed commissioners ignored rules that enhance and exploit such expertise.

The article identifies three consequences of such refusals to cultivate and apply expertise.  First, such abdication justifies removal under the FTC Act’s definition of cause.  Congress designed for cause restrictions to enhance and exploit expertise, and refusal to behave as an expert constitutes “neglect of duty,” one cause for removal.

Second, the removed commissioners’ refusal to behave as experts may impact their ability to obtain the equitable remedy of reinstatement.  Having breached their duties to cultivate and apply expertise, plaintiffs have unclean hands, barring equitable enforcement of protections designed to enhance such expertise.  Recognizing this defense is particularly appropriate here, where continued neglectful service as Commissioners would threaten public injury in the form of expertise-free decision making.

Third, the article supplements previous research concluding that, despite insulation from Presidential control, the Commission has not functioned in the nonpartisan, expert manner that Congress expected.  The assumption of nonpartisan expertise having proved false, Humphrey’s rationale no longer withstands analysis.  Absent some other rationale supporting such restrictions, Humphrey’s should be overruled.

title: Last-Mile PAYGo Energy: Allocating Support Across Fragile Payment Nodes in Developing Economies
affiliations: University of Pittsburgh - Katz Graduate School of Business and HEC Paris - Operations Management and Information Technology

detail.title: Last-Mile PAYGo Energy: Allocating Support Across Fragile Payment Nodes in Developing Economies
detail.abstract: Problem definition. Pay-as-you-go (PAYGo) solar providers deliver electricity through recurring mobile-money payments. When a local agent lacks electronic float, willing customers may be unable to pay, interrupting service and weakening repayment. Providers can soften contracts through grace, allowing temporary payment delays, or support payment nodes through interventions such as agent recruitment and float-rebalancing assistance. We study how a provider should choose contractual grace and allocate scarce node-level support across a heterogeneous network, and how targeted social subsidies can affect these decisions. Methodology/results. We develop a continuous-time portfolio model in which payment failures consist of a support-addressable common-shock component and an idiosyncratic customer-side component. We show that optimal support follows a composition-adjusted index that summarizes each node's private value, support-addressable failure, and cost-adjusted support productivity. The index illustrates why volume, raw-failure, or common-shock-share heuristics can misallocate support. In a calibrated baseline, these heuristics forgo 3.54-6.36% of firm value and leave about 11% of intermediate-node accounts exposed to avoidable lockout. The analysis also shows that grace and support can be complements or substitutes: grace preserves disrupted accounts, but can also reduce support's marginal role and dilute effective payoff. Consequently, the support index can be nonmonotone in grace. Finally, incorporating customer access value yields a social support index that reveals a private-viability gap: some nodes excluded under private optimality can warrant planner support. We characterize the optimal targeted subsidies and show how they can close this gap, generating win-win improvements in provider value, customer surplus, and social welfare. Managerial implications. Payment reliability is not merely a collections issue; it is an operational determinant of provider viability and household service access. PAYGo providers should target support using failure composition and support productivity, not only scale or observed fragility. Policymakers should target subsidies to nodes where social access value exceeds private support returns.

However, current research confirms that 83% of acquisitions fail to boost shareholder returns, with only 14% achieving significant success across strategic, operational, and financial measures simultaneously [1]. This paper introduces Quality Valuation Economics (QVEc), a discipline that quantifies an enterprise's structural integrity before capital is committed. By defining Quality as "Mindset in Action" [3], this conceptual framework explores how organizations accumulate Quality Equity or Quality Debt and introduces a multidimensional architecture for assessing the Quality of Operational Continuity (QoOC) and Quality of Value (QoV) without relying on deep mathematical disclosure. title: Optimizing Urban Traffic Flow Through a Hybrid Model-Based and Deep Learning Framework for Connected Multi-Intersection Control
affiliations: Moroccan School of Engineering Sciences, Université Paris Saclay and Moroccan School of Engineering Sciences

detail.title: Optimizing Urban Traffic Flow Through a Hybrid Model-Based and Deep Learning Framework for Connected Multi-Intersection Control
detail.abstract: The efficient management of traffic light intersections is a key factor that influences the fluidity of urban traffic flow. In this study, a new acyclic traffic signal control system  (TSCS) is presented that is designed to minimize vehicle waiting times by varying the duration of traffic light phases and the total cycle time according to the traffic situation, as long as the safety and structural constraints of the intersections are respected.  A reliable control signal system is defined by its accurate comprehension of the environment and its regard for communication among the structure's components. In this respect, the TSCS system has successfully controlled a network composed of nine intersections simultaneously by ensuring intercommunication and data exchange among the intersections.  The proposed approach is based on a mathematical modelization of the network interaction with the environment as a Markov decision process (MDP) where the reward is the average waiting time for all vehicles crossing the nine intersections. The action consists of selecting the next switching dates for all traffic lights, in order to transition towards a new status defined by the new lights states and resulting queue lengths. The aim of the system is to determine the optimal policy, which is the set of actions to be taken to achieve the minimum reward. For this reason, the policy iteration (PI) method is the appropriate resolution method. PI method tests every possible policy until it converges on the optimum policy. The PI resolution simulation in MATLAB has reduced the reward by up to 30\% compared with a non-adaptive system for a variety of situations collected from different locations.We combine the accuracy of model-based methods with the real-time feature of Deep learning By developing  a Deep Learning method based  on PI results as learning data, which minimized  the waiting times in real time.

title: Conditions for Coopetition of Farms in the Agri-Food Sector on the Example of the Warmińsko-Mazurskie Province

detail.title: Conditions for Coopetition of Farms in the Agri-Food Sector on the Example of the Warmińsko-Mazurskie Province
detail.abstract: The aim of the study was to identify the most important determinants of farms coopetition in the agri- -food sector on the example of the Warmińsko-Mazurskie Province. Using the survey questionnaire, the research was carried out in 2021 on a research sample of 155 entities (farms, economic self- -government units, trade associations, processing undertakings, and government agencies dealing with issues related to food economy and rural development had the largest share). The results show that the respondents were aware of the potential benefits of coopetition; they primarily pointed to the opportunities to increase sales, reduce costs, and gain greater bargaining power in relations with suppliers and recipients. Defining the basic barriers to the development of coopetition in the agri- -food sector, the respondents indicated, above all, low awareness of part of the business environment, the reluctance of companies to cooperate with each other, and the lack of coopetition development models. In the institutional dimension, a special role in the implementation of coopetition should be attributed to advisory entities, economic self-government, trade associations, and scientific institutions. Conditions for the development of farm coopetition in the Warmińsko-Mazurskie Province include not only endogenous, but above all exogenous factors shaping the possibilities of greater involvement of the surveyed entities in strategic cooperation in the agri-food sector. It was concluded that the coopetition gap of farms can be significantly reduced by greater involvement in integration processes, e.g., in the food industry. It is also very important to inspire integration activities by regulatory institutions related to the economic development of the region.

title: Capitalizing on Short-Term Rigidities: An ML Forecasting Solution for Small and Family Run Businesses
affiliations: Weston High School

detail.title: Capitalizing on Short-Term Rigidities: An ML Forecasting Solution for Small and Family Run Businesses
detail.abstract: In markets across the globe, small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and family-run businesses are always playing catch-up to larger, more established firms with dominance in trust, pricing, distribution, and production. SMEs and family-run businesses need weapons that will level the playing field. In this paper, we propose a six-week Machine Learning (ML) and Large Language Model (LLM) based forecasting pipeline, with the aim of providing short-term opportunities for SMEs and family-run businesses to capitalize on the rigidity of larger corporations. Tested on the Dutch Tulip Sector from June 13th to July 24th, 2025, we forecasted industry-related consumer sentiment, macroeconomic time series, and ecological indicators with robust ML models like an Extreme Gradient-Boosting Regressor (XGBoost), a Long Short-Term Memory Neural Network (LSTM), and a Random Forest (RF) respectively, interpreting forecasts with Meta’s Llama 3 8B Instruct into an six-week action plan. Very promising quantitative results were produced, including testing Root Mean Square Errors (RMSEs) of ~7.3884 average humidity (%), ~1.5382 for average temperature (ºC), and ~1.4658 for PM2.5 air pollutant levels (µg/m3). The practical results demonstrate the effectiveness of ML forecasting with LLM interpretation for exploiting short-term windows, taking market share away from larger companies. These results are important because on-target predictions of consumer-sentiment, ecological, and macroeconomic shifts in the short-term reveal when larger corporations are to have pain points in their operations

detail.abstract: We study whether trust causally affects attitudes toward paternalistic interventions. In an online experiment, we manipulate trust using an information prime. In a dyadic relationship, we measure both a stakeholder's willingness-to-accept a paternalistic intervention by an expert and the expert's willingness-to-intervene paternalistically in the stakeholder's freedom of choice. We find that higher trust increases the willingnessto-accept paternalistic interventions by raising the belief that the expert acts in stakeholder's best interests. However, although trust increases the expert's perceived authorization to intervene, it does not affect actual intervention behavior. Overall, the results highlight the role of intrinsic autonomy concerns in shaping attitudes toward paternalistic interventions.

detail.abstract: The judicial power to punish for contempt is a cornerstone in the judicial administration. The concept of contempt of court traces its roots back to ancient legal systems, where preserving the court's dignity and integrity was paramount. In the contemporary context, the relevance of this judicial power to punish for contempt is equally profound. In an era of digital communication and social media, the boundaries of contemptuous conduct have expanded, presenting new challenges to the judicious application of such powers. This article delves into the multifaceted dimensions of this judicial authority by examining its history and contemporary relevance. It explores the debates surrounding contempt of court in the present digital age, addressing issues related to freedom of speech, the role of the judiciary in safeguarding its authority, and the potential consequences of overzealous enforcement. In conclusion, the article offers an overview, drawing upon historical insights to shed light on its significance in present-day society. It underscores the delicate balance between protecting the sanctity of the legal process and upholding fundamental rights, making a compelling case for the continued examination and refinement of this vital aspect of the administration of justice.

detail.abstract:
The paper reviews 200 papers regarding environmentally adjusted analysis of agricultural efficiency
found in the Scopus database. based on the PRiSMa method the scope of the review was limited to
papers where efficiency is assessed with data envelopment analysis (DEA) or stochastic frontier analysis (SFA). The aim of this paper is to identify how efficiency analysis can be enhanced to take into
account environmental aspects of agricultural production and indicate the research trends and gaps.
Regarding the trends, most of the studies refer to agriculture in europe, with a noticeable increasing
trend in asia. the production directions under research mainly include crops or milk production, usually in the farm scale. It can also be observed that a typical economic efficiency model is developed
to include new environmentally detrimental inputs or undesirable outputs, such as fertilizing, climate
impact, crop protection, water footprint, and energy usage. the most common determinants were
farmers features, scale of production, intensification, agricultural practices, quality of the production environment, macroeconomic environment, specialization, environmental practices, and farm
features. The following research gaps were identified. The case studies of Africa and North America
are limited, like those at the field and local levels as well as those related to horticultural and animal production other than milk production. The SFA approaches are underdeveloped in comparison with DEA, like approaches other than additional inputs/outputs. In particular, the by-production approach seems promising. Limited attention has been paid to soil condition, biodiversity, waste generation in agriculture, and positive externalities provided by the agriculture. an interesting and less
investigated area in terms of performance determinants remain farmers’ behavioral features.

title: The Payment Term Paradox: A Theory of Credible Communication in Supply Chain Finance
affiliations: , University of Connecticut - Department of Operations & Information Management, School of Business, University of Connecticut and

detail.title: The Payment Term Paradox: A Theory of Credible Communication in Supply Chain Finance
detail.abstract: Demand forecasts can help suppliers align production with market conditions, but such forecasts are often informal, unverifiable, and strategically distorted. We study how payment terms in supply chain finance affect the credibility of this communication. In our model, an informed retailer sends a nonbinding demand forecast to a capital-constrained supplier, who chooses production and finances it through a combination of retailer prepayment and bank borrowing. The communication is cheap talk in that it is not verifiable and does not commit the retailer to realized demand, but it also defines the production and financing envelope within which the supplier operates. This institutional feature makes the prepayment ratio an informational governance device. First, we identify a payment term paradox. Increasing upfront payment does not monotonically improve incentive alignment. With little or no prepayment, the retailer bears limited pre-delivery exposure from inducing higher production and overstates demand. With near-complete prepayment, the retailer's upfront obligation becomes sufficiently large that a high-demand retailer understates demand to reduce her cash outlay. Truthful communication is therefore sustainable only for an intermediate range of partial prepayment. Second, financing conditions and payment terms interact: when bank financing becomes more costly or risky, a higher prepayment ratio is required to preserve credible communication. Within hybrid financing, a moderate increase in unit cost or financing risk can surprisingly raise all parties' profits by flipping the selected equilibrium from babbling to truthful communication. Finally, credible communication improves demand-production matching and can increase total supply chain surplus, but it need not benefit the supplier, because truthful low-demand reports activate a tighter production envelope that restricts upside in the high state. These findings show that payment terms in supply chain finance should be evaluated not only for their liquidity and risk-allocation effects, but also for their effect on the credibility of operational information.

title: The Organizational Cognitive Resonance & Alignment (O-CRA) Framework: A Multi-Dimensional Model for Quantifying Organizational AI Alignment

detail.title: The Organizational Cognitive Resonance & Alignment (O-CRA) Framework: A Multi-Dimensional Model for Quantifying Organizational AI Alignment
detail.abstract:
Organizations investing in generative AI face a paradox: different models feel distinct during interaction yet demonstrate surprising consensus on standard evaluation benchmarks. We explain this paradox by demonstrating that fundamental philosophical differences between AI systems emerge primarily in controversial edge cases, not in routine scenarios.

We introduce the Organizational Cognitive Resonance & Alignment (O-CRA) framework, which extends individual-level cognitive alignment to the organizational level across six dimensions: Strategic Intent Alignment, Cultural & Linguistic Synchronization, Systemic Process Integration, Governance & Safety Architecture, Institutional Knowledge Scaffolding, and ROI & Value Translation.

Our analysis evaluates 21 AI systems, 14 current and 7 historical versions, spanning major commercial providers, regional developers, and independent labs. Boundary testing across 151 organizational scenarios reveals a continuous philosophical spectrum from Strict Formalists (emphasizing compliance) to Helpful Pragmatists (emphasizing user empowerment), with a 51.6 percentage-point gap between extremes of current models (66.2% to 14.6%); the gap widens to 58.9 pp when including historical models.

Approximately half of all tests expose measurable philosophical divergence between models, with Strategic Intent Alignment emerging as both the most philosophically divisive dimension and the primary driver of philosophical shifts across versions.

Longitudinal analysis across seven version pairs reveals pervasive volatility: six of seven pairs crossed category boundaries, with four moving toward stricter evaluation. Most dramatically, Grok crossed two category boundaries in a single update, a −45.0 pp shift from Helpful Pragmatist to Strict Formalist. Only DeepSeek maintained its category across versions.

These findings shift organizational AI strategy from generic capability assessment to philosophical compatibility matching. We provide evidence-based guidance for selecting AI systems based on alignment with organizational values and risk tolerance, and demonstrate that philosophical positioning requires continuous monitoring rather than one-time assessment.

detail.abstract:
Vulnerability exploitation now outpaces remediation by an order of magnitude. The 2024 Verizon DBIR found that exploitation as an initial breach vector rose 180 percent year-over-year, with mass exploitation of CISA KEV entries beginning roughly five days after publication. Organizations need approximately 55 days to remediate half of their critical vulnerabilities, and the 2025 DBIR shows the gap continuing to widen. Automated defensive capabilities sufficient to close this gap have matured within the same three-year window, from Google's 2024 demonstration of LLM-based patching at scale to DeepMind's CodeMender shipping 72 upstream fixes to critical open-source projects in late 2025, alongside the broad release of AIxCC finalist platforms. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 does not currently provide control language authorizing or constraining these capabilities as distinct functions, and authorization practice across the federal and contractor populations reflects that gap. 
This paper proposes two new control enhancements: RA-5(12) Automated Security Analysis Integration and CM-3(9) Authorized Automated Remediation. Both are written to be technology-neutral at the control text level, with representative implementations (SIEM with advanced analytics, Cyber Reasoning Systems, AIenabled vulnerability analysis platforms) named in discussion text in the existing 800-53 pattern. CM-3(9) follows the authorization model already used for SOAR: the capability and its operating envelope are authorized as part of the system security plan, and individual actions within the envelope are accountable through audit but not individually reviewable. Corresponding baseline assignments in SP 800-53B place RA-5(12) at Moderate and High, and CM-3(9) at High only, with a derived requirement carried into SP 800-171 Rev 3.
The proposal addresses the inverse of the problem space covered by the current NIST AI portfolio. The AI RMF, COSAiS, SP 800-218A, NIST AI 100-2, and draft AI 800-1 secure AI systems and manage AI-induced risk. The controls proposed here cover the use of automated capabilities, AI-enabled or otherwise, to manage cyber risk in any system. This is a gap rather than a duplication, and the case for closing it during the current revision cycle rests on the documented exploitation-versus-remediation asymmetry combined with the proliferation trajectory of agentic AI in both offensive and defensive postures.

title: Trading Halt Discretion and Market Quality: Evidence from a Regulatory Reform

detail.title: Trading Halt Discretion and Market Quality: Evidence from a Regulatory Reform
detail.abstract: This paper studies investor responses to China's 2018 trading halt reform, which restricted listed firms' discretion to initiate and extend trading suspensions. Using a difference-indifferences design, I compare firms with intensive pre-reform halt usage to matched firms with no pre-reform suspensions. Treated firms experience a positive stock price reaction and increased trading activity following the reform. However, this favourable average response is accompanied by greater investor disagreement and weaker short-run market quality, reflected in higher volatility, greater illiquidity, and slower price discovery. Additional tests suggest that disagreement reflects uncertainty about policy enforcement and heterogeneity in firms' historical halt usage: the positive price reaction is stronger when past halts are more likely to be perceived as costly, opportunistic, or less beneficial to investors. The evidence highlights a market-design trade-off in which restricting firm-level halt discretion generates favourable average market responses while temporarily increasing disagreement and impairing market quality.

detail.abstract: The public conversation about artificial intelligence is dominated by model capability-parameter counts, benchmark scores, and the race to build ever-larger frontier systems. This paper argues that this framing misidentifies where durable advantage actually accrues. Drawing on recent empirical evidence that roughly ninety-five percent of enterprise generative-AI pilots fail to deliver measurable business impact, and that the dominant causes are integration, data quality, and governance rather than model quality, it advances a practitioner thesis: AI leadership-whether for a firm or a nation-will be determined less by who builds the most powerful model than by who can integrate AI responsibly into real institutional workflows. The paper synthesizes the author's experience across large-scale enterprise modernization, data-migration, and robotic-process-automation programs with the current literature on AI adoption failure and AI governance. It presents generalized practitioner cases and names the recurring failure modes and architectural antipatterns through which integration fails in production. It introduces a seven-layer model-the Accountable Integration Stack-spanning automation beyond the clean core, orchestration, governance, reconciliation, exception handling, escalation routing, and auditability, terminating in human accountability, and aligns it with established governance guidance such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. It argues that the rise of agentic AI makes these integration layers more decisive rather than less, confronts the strongest counterargument from rising frontier capability, and extends the analysis to national policy. The paper concludes that national AI capability is fundamentally an institutional capability: the capacity to deploy AI at scale with transparency, governance, and human accountability. The argument is offered as a practitioner perspective grounded in published evidence, not as original empirical research; its limitations and scope are stated explicitly.

title: Allocating Limited Outreach Capacity: Distinguishing Donor Responsiveness from Donor Value

detail.title: Allocating Limited Outreach Capacity: Distinguishing Donor Responsiveness from Donor Value
detail.abstract: Annual giving programs face a recurring customer-facing operations challenge: how to allocate limited outreach capacity across donors and channels when outreach efforts differ in cost, scalability, and effectiveness. This problem cannot be solved by predicting donation levels alone, because donors with high expected giving are not necessarily those whose contributions are most responsive to outreach. We develop a Bayesian framework for annual giving operations that distinguishes donor responsiveness from donor value. Building on the Cragg model, the framework separates participation and donation-amount decisions, accommodates many true zeros and highly skewed positive contributions, allows outreach effects to vary across donors, channels, and time, and accounts for endogenous outreach assignment. We apply the framework to donorlevel annual giving records from a major U.S. public university foundation over an 18-year period. The framework reveals substantial heterogeneity in donor-level responsiveness and shows that donor value and outreach responsiveness are related but distinct. Compared with a benchmark Cragg model, our framework improves predictive accuracy, particularly for donors who receive more outreach and those with irregular giving patterns. In fixed-budget simulations, an optimized allocation policy guided by estimated donor responsiveness generates at least $300,000 more in total expected donations, roughly a 12% improvement, than benchmark policies based on prior year giving or predicted donor value. The study contributes to nonprofit operations by showing how recurring outreach operations can prioritize limited contact resources based on responsiveness rather than expected giving alone.
