detail.abstract: This study analyzes the current implementation of voluntary corporate carbon governance. We assess the commitments, actions, and emissions reported by firms operating in four industrial sectors (energy, automobiles, technology, and food) from 2018 to 2022. We analyze trends in absolute carbon emissions and carbon intensity and then present a comparative assessment of firms within the technology sector. We find that current carbon governance systems have had limited impact, as absolute carbon emissions remain flat or are rising across sectors. Underlying information systems have produced data that neither guides internal decisions effectively nor enables external accountability. This governance system is now being formalized into regulations in the European Union, United States, and Asia. These regulations risk failure unless they are modified to generate carbon data that is material, consistent, and actionable at the resolution and cadence of business decisions, while supporting external oversight.

title: The Best Card Paradox: Why the Card You Choose Is Almost Never the Card You Use

detail.title: The Best Card Paradox: Why the Card You Choose Is Almost Never the Card You Use
detail.abstract: For most consumers, the credit card they choose is not the credit card they end up benefiting from. Premium cards with $550 to $695 annual fees deliver benefit envelopes that, on paper, more than justify the cost. In practice, between 55 and 70 percent of premium cardholders fail to recoup the annual fee in any given year, depending on the survey methodology and product cohort. Rotating-category cash-back cards advertise headline rates of 5 percent but deliver realized returns frequently below 2 percent. Signup bonuses with spending thresholds in the $4,000 range are forfeited by a meaningful share of new-account cohorts. The pattern is too consistent across surveys, issuers, and product categories to be attributable to consumer-side noise. It is a structural feature of how the market operates, and it has consequences for consumer welfare that disclosurebased regulation has not addressed and that algorithmic recommendation systems, as currently designed, have not been built to remediate. This paper develops a two-stage model in which consumer value capture is the product of a selection stage (which card to hold) and a realization stage (how much of its benefit envelope the consumer actually uses), formalizes the resulting decomposition of expected welfare, and argues that the current generation of recommendation engines is solving only the first half of the consumer's actual problem. The selection stage is well-understood, well-tooled, and largely solved. The realization stage is where most of the value lives, and it has been almost entirely ignored. The paper draws on the behavioural economics literature on choice overload, hyperbolic discounting, mental accounting, and limited attention; on the empirical literature on consumer financial decision-making; on industry survey data from Bankrate, J.D. Power, and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's biennial market reports; and on the author's own experience building a Canadian credit card comparison platform. The argument has both descriptive and prescriptive content. Descriptively, the realization gap is large, systematic, and monetized by issuers. Prescriptively, an algorithmic recommendation system that incorporates a realizationcoefficient estimate, rather than ranking products on attribute value alone, can close a significant fraction of the gap and produce welfare improvements that the current regulatory framework has been unable to deliver.

title: The Annual Fee Inversion: Why a $695 Credit Card Can Cost Less than a Free One, and Why the Market Cannot Tell You in Advance

detail.title: The Annual Fee Inversion: Why a $695 Credit Card Can Cost Less than a Free One, and Why the Market Cannot Tell You in Advance
detail.abstract: For a narrowly defined slice of the cardholder population, the most expensive consumer credit card products in the US market deliver net realized returns substantially above their annual fees. For the remainder of the population, the same products deliver net realized losses, often equal to the full annual fee. The credit card market shows no efficient mechanism to sort consumers between the two groups in advance of purchase. This paper develops a formal account of the resulting cross-subsidy, in which the underutilizing majority finances the over-utilizing minority and the issuer retains a margin in the middle. The structure is similar to the gym membership puzzle of DellaVigna and Malmendier (2006), to the dominated plan choice problem in health insurance (Bhargava, Loewenstein and Sydnor, 2017), and to the screening-by-naivete equilibrium of Heidhues and Koszegi (2010), and it generalizes to a class of markets where firms profit from systematic consumer misforecasts. Three features of the credit card market sustain the equilibrium: realization rates are not observable to consumers at the point of decision, comparison platforms collect attribute data but not behavioural data, and issuers have no incentive to disclose realization patterns. Each of the three barriers is, with the right algorithmic and regulatory infrastructure, addressable. The paper closes with a discussion of how Section 1033 personal financial data rights, combined with comparison platforms that build on behavioural signal extraction, can perform the sort that the market currently does not.

title: The Identification Gap: A Historical Case for Fabric-Native Identity Encoding

detail.title: The Identification Gap: A Historical Case for Fabric-Native Identity Encoding
detail.abstract:
This white paper presents a chronological and thematic argument demonstrating that every existing method of human identification — physical tags, electronic IFF systems, visual clothing descriptors, and fabric-embedded digital technologies — shares a single, fundamental vulnerability: the identifier is structurally separate from the person, and that separation fails under the conditions that matter most. T

racing identification failures from the Civil War through the 2026 Kuwait friendly-fire incident, from wilderness SAR operations to peer-reviewed materials science literature, this paper establishes the complete problem landscape that a fabric-native, self-reliant, encryption-capable identity medium was invented to solve. 

That invention — currently pending before the USPTO under the filing “A System and Method for Real-Time Binary Translation on Apparel” — is the subject of this research series. This document serves as the foundational source archive and argument structure for a vertical patent strategy encompassing multiple derivative applications.

title: The Heart of Monetary Economics: A Novel Diagram Depicting the Relationships between Aggregate Monetary Variables
affiliations: Clayton State University - College of Business

detail.title: The Heart of Monetary Economics: A Novel Diagram Depicting the Relationships between Aggregate Monetary Variables
detail.abstract: This work introduces the heart of monetary economics, a simple figure that contains more information than the Venn diagram that shows how the monetary base and money supply have currency in circulation as their intersection. A distinguishing feature of the heart is that it illustrates how the net amount of financial capital generated by depository institutions equals the difference between the money supply and the monetary base. As such, the figure may aid students learning about money creation. This work also points out a nearly identical figure that contains the same information as the heart. The paper also provides a proof that these two figures are the only two with their general shape consistent with the relationships they display.

title: Pricing Regulatory Risk: Evidence from U.S.-Listed Chinese Stocks under the HFCAA

detail.title: Pricing Regulatory Risk: Evidence from U.S.-Listed Chinese Stocks under the HFCAA
detail.abstract: This study examines when and how the regulatory risk created by the Holding Foreign Companies Accountable Act (HFCAA) became credible enough to be priced by investors in U.S.-listed Chinese equities. The HFCAA-by requiring that issuers' auditors submit to inspection by the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) or face eventual delisting-converted a long-standing conflict over cross-border audit access into a concrete delisting threat, embedded within the broader process of U.S.-China financial decoupling. Our central premise is that such a threat is not priced at the moment of legislative enactment, but rather as its enforceability and operational credibility become apparent to the market. Using daily returns for a sample of 58 U.S.-listed Chinese firms (American Depositary Receipts and ordinary shares), we conduct an event study around seven HFCAA-related regulatory milestones spanning May 2020 to December 2022, estimating abnormal returns within a market-model framework benchmarked to the NASDAQ Composite Index. The results indicate that the market reacted not to legislative form but to the credibility of regulatory commitment: statutory enactment elicited a near-zero response, whereas the operationalization of the implementation framework produced the largest and most consistent negative abnormal returns. Later escalation events deepened the repricing, while the subsequent reduction of near-term delisting risk in December 2022 generated an attenuated, de-escalatory response. By tracing the pricing of institutional risk across the HFCAA's evolution from legislative proposal to operational enforcement, the study situates regulatory-risk pricing within the wider dynamics of U.S.-China strategic rivalry, audit-access conflict, and crossborder capital flows. It thereby contributes to the literature on political risk, regulatory uncertainty, and international asset pricing under conditions of financial decoupling.

title: Does Oil Price Uncertainty Impact Corporate Innovation? Insights from Corporate Culture
affiliations: Sasin GIBA, Pennsylvania State University - School of Graduate Professional Studies (SGPS) and Mahidol University International College (MUIC)

detail.title: Does Oil Price Uncertainty Impact Corporate Innovation? Insights from Corporate Culture
detail.abstract: We examine the critical impact of oil price uncertainty on corporate innovation culture. We employ a unique measure of corporate innovation derived from textual analysis of earnings call transcripts, offering a more comprehensive perspective on innovation than traditional metrics like R&D expenditures and patents. The findings reveal a significant negative effect of oil price uncertainty on corporate innovation, indicating that firms tend to scale back innovation activities in response to heightened uncertainty. Since we account for overall economic uncertainty, the observed effect of oil price uncertainty on innovation is distinct and goes beyond the influence of general economic conditions. Importantly, firms where innovation is more critical to profitability experience a smaller decline in innovation when faced with oil price uncertainty. This research contributes to the understanding of how external economic factors, particularly oil price volatility, influence corporate innovation strategies and highlights the differential impact across firms based on the strategic importance of innovation.

title: Trump's Leadership: Repeating Disastrous Economic Policy
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Trump's Leadership: Repeating Disastrous Economic Policy

detail.abstract: This paper examines the flaws of Trump’s economic policy, connecting it to post-WWI American history to show how those policy mistakes have already been made by previous conservative leaders, and should not have been repeated. In particular, this paper focuses on three particular policies: Tariffs, deregulation, and income tax cuts. Heavy tariffs were already proved to be dangerous with Hoover’s Smoot-Harley tariff, and Trump’s tariffs are not much better, coming with many issues such as retaliatory tariffs that hurt American businesses rather than help them. Rather than help grow the US economy, Trump’s tariffs were found to have the potential to suppress its growth. Deregulation, while it may help sometimes, was found to have its own issues in Reagan’s time, and Trump’s deregulation may repeat that again, hurting many American workers by rolling back on union protection laws, and taking away from their ability to be prepared for a financial crisis. Finally, Trump’s tax cuts, just like George W. Bush’s tax cuts, were found to be strictly helping the people who needed it the least, while plunging the nation into even greater debt, something future generations may have to pay for at an unimaginable price. All of these mistakes could have been avoided by learning from history, and now, the US economy may pay for it.

title: Zakāh as Tithe: Fiscal Engineering in Early Islamic Jurisprudence
affiliations: Rice University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Zakāh as Tithe: Fiscal Engineering in Early Islamic Jurisprudence
detail.abstract: The classical zakāh schedule is traditionally presented as a wealth tax with four rates (bracketed for livestock), each anchored in a separate canonical text. I recharacterize the schedule as a net-income tithe. The agrarian yield tithe (traditionally an exception within a wealth-tax system) is taken as the organizing principle. The zakāh tithing base is realized or presumptive yield, scaled down by a cost offset or up by a windfall premium. The schedule is thus seen as an early effort to serve the objectives later formalized in modern optimal-tax theory: comprehensive income taxation, production-efficiency netting-out, neutrality across asset classes, and heavy taxation of windfall rents. Its rate-graded, yield-based, cost-adjusted form adapted earlier Near Eastern fiscal administrative practice, e.g., kharāj, over the eighth and ninth centuries. Later jurists classified this engineered fiscal schedule as devotional worship, insulating it from useful economic analysis and public-policy revision.

title: Template Governance and Value Capture in Intermediaries: Evidence from Pharmacy Benefit Managers
affiliations: University of Utah - David Eccles School of Business and Syracuse University - Whitman School of Management

detail.title: Template Governance and Value Capture in Intermediaries: Evidence from Pharmacy Benefit Managers

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Despite a large literature on governance design, there is scant theoretical or empirical attention to the use of standardized templates paired with formal exception processes ("template governance") and its strategic implications in markets where intermediaries serve heterogeneous downstream coalitions and bargain on their behalf with upstream suppliers. In this study, we conceptualize template governance as a distinct strategic instrument that jointly disciplines downstream coalition participation and the credibility of upstream disagreement payoffs, and we examine empirically how intermediaries design and revise templates in response to client and supplier behavior. Leveraging novel commercial drug insurance data on pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) from 2011-2019, we find that national formulary templates evolve toward prior client deviations with disproportionate weight on large clients, that larger and more capable clients deviate more and adopt templates less often, that intermediaries selectively resist accommodation on drugs where upstream bargaining stakes are highest, and that template fit strongly predicts subsequent relationship stability. Further, evidence from the Express Scripts-Medco merger reinforces these mechanisms, highlighting how template governance shapes coalition formation and value appropriation in intermediated markets.

title: Chinese Export Gains, EU Export Losses, and Russian Import Reorientation after the 2022 Sanctions
affiliations: Research Institute of Industrial Economics (IFN)

detail.title: Chinese Export Gains, EU Export Losses, and Russian Import Reorientation after the 2022 Sanctions

declarations.funderStatement: I gratefully acknowledge financial support from Jan Wallander and Tom Hedelius stiftelse (P23-0186) and from Marianne and Marcus Wallenberg Foundation (2024.0019)

publicationDetails.journalName: Research Institute of Industrial Economics (IFN) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper examines how Russian imports were reoriented after the 2022 sanctions. Using annual bilateral trade data at the product level, it asks whether direct Chinese export gains to Russia were concentrated in the same product lines in which EU exports to Russia declined. It also studies rerouting through Hong Kong, Armenia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Türkiye. The results point to substantial post-2022 import reorientation in Russia. Direct Chinese export gains are larger in product lines where Russia had depended more heavily on EU suppliers before the sanctions. Including transit-linked flows strengthens this relationship and points to broader rerouting through intermediary economies in those same product lines. In sanction-relevant goods, direct Chinese gains offset only part of the EU shortfall, while intermediary-country channels account for a substantial additional share. On the EU side, product-level evidence also suggests that some of the lost Russian market was absorbed through higher exports of the same products to other non-transit destinations. The evidence is therefore consistent with partial direct substitution by China, broader rerouting through intermediary economies, and partial outward redirection by EU exporters, not full replacement of lost EU exports.

title: Municipal Bond Volatility: Measurement, Explanations, and Implications
affiliations: University of Chicago, University of Chicago and University of Chicago, Harris School of Public Policy, Center for Municipal Finance

detail.title: Municipal Bond Volatility: Measurement, Explanations, and Implications
detail.abstract: Municipal bonds have a reputation as a stable, low-volatility asset class, but that reputation has been tested repeatedly over the past decade by episodes of sharp market dislocation. Using random forest modeling on more than a dozen data sources, we document what has driven this increase in volatility and what it means for issuers and investors. We find that three overlapping forces are responsible: a structural shift in the investor base toward exchange-traded funds and separately managed accounts that amplifies price movements during periods of stress; the growing transmission of Treasury market volatility into municipal prices; and investor sentiment and policy uncertainty that appear to amplify rather than independently drive volatility. These findings matter directly to issuers because elevated volatility raises borrowing costs, and to investors because the municipal market is increasingly sensitive to forces that have little to do with the credit quality of the underlying bonds.

title: Ordo-Liberalism for the Digital Age -Heike Schweitzer's "Decentralized Coordination Order"
affiliations: Université de Montréal

detail.title: Ordo-Liberalism for the Digital Age -Heike Schweitzer's "Decentralized Coordination Order"

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Nothing to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: No financial support.

detail.abstract: Heike Schweitzer’s “decentralized coordination order” rejuvenates ordo-liberal thought. Yet her analysis is hampered by reliance on market failure as the linchpin between economics and law. A matrix of market theories – with efficiency-discovery and constructivist-naturalist axes – shows that the theoretical space for law is much larger than simply remedying market failure. In our digital economy, physical or virtual marketplaces are being replaced by automated matchmaking, driven by platforms and agentic AI. This development reveals and threatens implicit assumptions that underpinned more naturalist/spontaneous market theories. The question is then not so much whether markets fail, but whether they are operative. A more constructivist mechanism design approach should be followed, where law takes a larger role in ensuring that markets work at all. At stake is not only the presence of consumer surplus from an efficiency-based perspective, but the very survival of markets as decentralized discovery mechanisms.

title: Fighting for Growth: Labor Scarcity and Technological Progress during the British Industrial Revolution
affiliations: University of Zurich - UBS International Center of Economics in Society, University of Zurich and University of Glasgow

detail.title: Fighting for Growth: Labor Scarcity and Technological Progress during the British Industrial Revolution

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.

detail.abstract: New data and evidence demonstrate a link between labor scarcity and the adoption of labor-saving technology in industrializing England. During the Napoleonic Wars, up to 10-14% of the male population served in the armed forces. Where recruitment was heavy, more machines economizing on labor were adopted. Naval recruitment, instrumented by warships' coastal access, provides exogenous shocks to labor scarcity. These shocks led to the adoption of labor-saving machines, but not non-labor-saving technologies. Importantly, there is a synergy between skill abundance and labor scarcity-where labor shortages boosted machine adoption, technology afterwards improved more rapidly.

title:
Internalizing Externalities: 
An Analysis of Pigovian Taxes and Environmental Policy Failures

detail.title:
Internalizing Externalities: 
An Analysis of Pigovian Taxes and Environmental Policy Failures
detail.abstract: This report examines the theoretical foundations and practical limitations of Pigovian taxation as a mechanism for internalising negative externalities in environmental policy. Drawing on three comparative case studies-Ireland's plastic bag levy, Spain's Royal Decree 900/2015 (the "Sun Tax"), and London's evolving congestion and emission charge regime-the analysis identifies recurring causes of policy failure, including metric misspecification, regressive distributional effects, and unintended substitution effects. The findings suggest that effective environmental taxation requires precise targeting of the harmful externality, financial equity, elimination of exemptions that distort behaviour, and reinvestment of revenues into viable cleaner alternatives.

title: The Effects of Minimum Wage Increases on Employment and Firm Dynamics in Puerto Rico

detail.title: The Effects of Minimum Wage Increases on Employment and Firm Dynamics in Puerto Rico

detail.abstract: Recent research has increasingly questioned the canonical prediction that minimum wages have negative effects on employment. This paper studies Puerto Rico's Act 47-2021, which raised the island's minimum wage by 44.8% in three steps between 2022 and 2024, the largest minimum wage shock in any U.S. jurisdiction in recent decades. Puerto Rico presents a uniquely powerful natural experiment: as a U.S. territory subject to the federal Fair Labor Standards Act but with a Kaitz ratio of approximately 0.60, the highest of any U.S. jurisdiction, it sits at the theoretical boundary where competing models make opposing predictions. Using several econometric specifications, I estimate causal effects on total nonfarm employment, manufacturing productivity, and business establishments across a twelve-year inter-sectoral panel. I find no evidence that Act 47-2021 reduced total nonfarm employment, with results directionally pointing towards positive employment gains though statistically indistinguishable from zero.

title: Household Bargaining and Desistance from Crime

detail.title: Household Bargaining and Desistance from Crime
detail.abstract: Family formation is associated with sharp declines in men's criminal activity, but the underlying mechanisms remain underexplored. This paper proposes and tests an intrahousehold bargaining mechanism. Entering a union, whether through cohabitation or marriage, brings otherwise unconstrained risky behaviors under joint decision-making. Partner disapproval creates demand for change, while bargaining power provides leverage to enforce it. Using individual-level panel data from the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1997 (NLSY97) linked to gender-specific local labor demand shocks, I show that improvements in women's relative labor market opportunities, used as a proxy for bargaining power, reduce their male partners' likelihood of arrest. The largest declines occur among high-risk men paired with high-leverage female partners. The effects are at least as strong for cohabitation as for marriage, consistent with a bargaining-based mechanism of desistance rather than explanations based solely on selection into unions or identity change.

title: From Consideration to Action: The Last-Minute Conflict in the Disposition Effect
affiliations: Peking University - Guanghua School of Management, Peking University - Guanghua School of Management, Peking University - Guanghua School of Management and Monash University - Department of Banking and Finance

detail.title: From Consideration to Action: The Last-Minute Conflict in the Disposition Effect
detail.abstract: This paper compares investors' actual selling behavior with their revealed selling consideration using granular browsing and transaction data, offering a new perspective on the disposition effect. We find that actual selling behavior diverges from revealed consideration, with a substantial portion of the disposition effect arising at the final order-submission stage. Submission actions made within less than two minutes account for roughly half of the documented disposition effect. These findings suggest that this last-minute disposition effect stems from a conflict between executing intended sales and reluctance to realize losses, rather than from a coherent, preconceived preference. We further document that investors disproportionately realize small gains that have recently switched from losses, consistent with an attempt to escape from this conflict.

title: Who Hires Whom? Entrepreneurial Backgrounds and Labor Market Opportunities
affiliations: University of Utah - David Eccles School of Business and London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) - Department of Economics

detail.title: Who Hires Whom? Entrepreneurial Backgrounds and Labor Market Opportunities
detail.abstract: What are the implications of unequal access to entrepreneurial careers for labor markets? Using data from the U.S. Census and LinkedIn profiles, we document that entrepreneurs are significantly more likely to hire workers from similar social backgrounds (gender, race, age, education, etc.). These effects are quantitatively large across several demographic dimensions. For example, female employee share at female founded startups is 36.4pp higher after controlling for industry-by-metro area-by-cohort fixed effects, with corresponding estimates of 51.2pp for Blacks, 37.3pp for Hispanics, and 11.3pp for non-college individuals. Large effects are present in high-growth startups, across industries and occupations, and remain stable across new firm cohorts. In addition, we find that these differences persist out to at least 20 years. We use wage data and an AKM research design to untangle whether the relative differences are driven by labor demand or labor supply effects. We find that demand drives the differences: group-specific wage decompositions show that new firms pay higher relative wages to individuals from similar backgrounds to the entrepreneur. Using these estimates, we calibrate a model of entrepreneurship with heterogeneous ability and production functions using our estimates, and assess the impacts on relative wage from reducing access barriers to entrepreneurship.

title:
Mitigating Deregulation:
 The Role of Supervision
affiliations: Bocconi University - Department of Finance, Bocconi University - Department of Finance, Bocconi University - Department of Finance and Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title:
Mitigating Deregulation:
 The Role of Supervision
detail.abstract: We study how regulation and supervision interact. Exploiting the 2018-2019 relaxation of liquidity requirements for US mid-sized banks, we show that affected banks experienced a deterioration in liquidity. At the same time, using confidential data from the Federal Reserve on supervisory hours, we document that these banks were subject to an increase in supervisory examination activity. The increase in supervisory intensity mitigates the deterioration in liquidity. These effects are stronger in districts where supervisors oversee fewer banks and have longer tenure. Preliminary evidence also suggests that deregulated banks expand lending, without a corresponding increase in other measures of risk. These findings suggest that supervision can partially substitute for regulatory discipline and highlight the importance of supervisory capacity for financial stability.

title: Posterior Concentration for the Euclidean Traveling Salesman Problem
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and George Mason University

detail.title: Posterior Concentration for the Euclidean Traveling Salesman Problem
detail.abstract: We develop a Bayesian treatment of the Euclidean traveling salesman problem (ETSP). The object of study is the Gibbs-Boltzmann measure π λ (σ) ∝ exp(-λL(σ)) on the symmetric group S n , where L(σ) is the length of a tour through n points drawn independently and uniformly from the unit square, and λ is an inverse temperature that plays the role of a posterior precision. The classical theorem of Beardwood, Halton, and Hammersley shows that the optimal tour length, normalized by √ n, converges almost surely to a universal constant β 2 ; the algorithm of Halton and Terada attains this limit by a deterministic strip construction running in near-linear time. We ask what posterior simulation adds to this picture, and prove four results. First, we identify the sharp temperature schedule for which the posterior concentrates on tours of near-optimal length: the threshold is λ n /(√ n log n) → ∞, with a matching converse. Second, we recast the Halton-Terada strip construction as one trajectory of a sequential Monte Carlo particle filter and give a finite-sample error bound for the randomized version. Third, we introduce a probit relaxation of the edge-indicator representation of ETSP and prove that the associated Pólya-Gamma Gibbs sampler is geometrically ergodic. Fourth, we analyze a control-variate estimator of β 2 built from Halton's low-discrepancy sequence. Simulations confirm the qualitative predictions of all four theorems and delineate the gap between the asymptotic theory and finite-sample behavior. The development connects the probabilistic analysis of combinatorial optimization to the modern Bayesian computational toolkit, and isolates one outstanding question-the mixing time of local Metropolis dynamics-as an open problem.

title: Monte Carlo Methods for Counting Self-Avoiding Walks: A Literature Review
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and George Mason University

detail.title: Monte Carlo Methods for Counting Self-Avoiding Walks: A Literature Review
detail.abstract: The self-avoiding walk (SAW) is a deceptively simple object whose enumeration c n encodes deep information about polymer statistics, critical phenomena, and the connective constant µ = lim n→∞ c 1/n n. Exact enumeration is feasible only out to modest n, so Monte Carlo has long been the workhorse for estimating c n and the critical exponents γ, ν. This review surveys the literature from the original RosenbluthRosenbluth chain-growth method (1955) through PERM, the pivot algorithm, sequential Monte Carlo with resampling, stochastic enumeration, and rigorous methods (lace expansion, SchrammLoewner evolution, parafermionic observables). Particular attention is paid to the unifying FeynmanKac/SMC perspective and to opportunities for the moderate-deviation-principle and generative-Bayesiancomputation programs to contribute.

title: Women's Equality in Canada: Sex in Law, Gender in Policy
affiliations: Queen's University (Canada), Faculty of Law

detail.title: Women's Equality in Canada: Sex in Law, Gender in Policy

declarations.funderStatement: The author acknowledges funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council, the Canadian Bar Association Law for the Future Fund, the Queen’s University Fund for Scholarly Research, and the Queen’s Law Research Fellowship.

detail.abstract: This article explores a divergence between the language used to advance women's equality in human rights law and the language used in federal policy and information practice. In international and domestic legal frameworks, the word sex has long functioned as the central characteristic for protecting women's rights and advancing women's equality. While legislated legal protections for women remain grounded in sex, in Canadian federal policy women's equality is framed as gender equality. Over time, use of the word gender-and the focus of gender equality-has evolved to extend beyond the categories of women and men. In policy, gender is distinguished from sex and increasingly prioritized over sex, while sex data is often obscured. The result is a definitional and conceptual misalignment between legal frameworks (where women's equality is pursued using the word sex) and policy (where women's equality is pursued using the word gender). This article examines the current divergence between Canada's use of sex-based legal protections and gender-based administrative governance as a foundation for critically considering the consequences for women's equality.

title: Perelman's Entropy, Dual Densities, and the Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, George Mason University and

detail.title: Perelman's Entropy, Dual Densities, and the Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle
detail.abstract:
We establish a unified framework connecting Perelman's W-entropy functional from Ricci flow geometry, scale mixtures of normals (SMN) and the horseshoe prior in Bayesian statistics, Good's Fisher dual density, Gneiting's spectral duality, and the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. On flat R n , our central decomposition is 
                       W(u, τ) = τ I(u)-n 2τ-KL u ∥ N (0, 2τ I) ≥ 0, 
identifying W as Fisher information excess minus KL divergence from the Gaussian, and as the excess of the position-momentum entropy sum above the Heisenberg minimum. Our main result is a fully probabilistic proof of W-monotonicity: the backward heat kernel is the transition density of X τ = B Sτ (Brownian motion subordinated by S), the reduced volume equals Ṽ (τ) = e-τ ψ(n/(2τ))+n/2 , and monotonicity is equivalent to the complete Bernstein property ψ(s) ≥ sψ ′ (s), replacing Perelman's tensor Frobenius norm with a single scalar inequality. Curvature enters as a Feynman-Kac tilt. We further develop the SMN-HCM-Thorin hierarchy: the horseshoe has Laplace transform e sτ 2 E 1 (sτ 2), Cauchy Thorin measure [π(u + τ 2)]-1 du, and W-complexity n 2 | log τ |, the logarithmic divergence that determines the minimax-optimal scale τ * ≍ s log(n/s)/n. Five further problems are resolved: a curved-space spectral SMN theory, the horseshoe logarithmic soliton, a quantum Bayesian W Q , a Perelman-level entropy power inequality, and a W-minimax identity.

title:
Financing Innovation: 
A Hurdle Rate Theory of Inventive Procyclicality
affiliations: Indiana University, , University of Hamburg, Syracuse University - Whitman School of Management and University of Bergamo

detail.title:
Financing Innovation: 
A Hurdle Rate Theory of Inventive Procyclicality
detail.abstract: Schumpeterian arguments of creative destruction predict that innovation is countercyclical. However, empirical findings demonstrate the contrary. We apply corporate finance principles to innovation economics and propose a hurdle-rate theory of inventive procyclicality. Macroeconomic episodes of high equity risk premia (ERP) hinder innovation in our 1977-2018 sample of U.S. firms because many R&D projects fail to pass corporate budgeting decisions when the aggregate discount rate is high. We exploit the staggered variation in state-level R&D tax credits in difference-indifferences analyses to establish a causal link between the ERP and patent value. In line with our hurdle-rate theory, we show that high-ERP episodes hurt those firms more that focus on exploratory search than their exploitative counterparts. Consistent evidence suggests that the hurdle rate effect is less pronounced in firms with financial slack, weak product market competition, and high institutional investor ownership.

title: Powering Ahead: Comparing Electricity Prices Across Canada
affiliations: and

detail.title: Powering Ahead: Comparing Electricity Prices Across Canada
detail.abstract:
• This Commentary compares electricity prices across Canadian provinces between 2018 and 2023, examining overall system costs and the prices paid by residential, commercial, and industrial consumers. Provinces with large hydroelectric systems generally recorded the lowest costs, while Alberta, Newfoundland and Labrador, Nova Scotia, and Ontario had the highest system costs in 2023.
  • Provincial rate structures distribute electricity costs differently across consumer classes. In most provinces, industrial consumers paid the lowest unit costs, while residential and small business consumers paid the highest. Ontario remained an exception because government mitigation programs reduced residential and small business costs relative to larger commercial and industrial consumers.
  • Most provinces saw declining electricity system costs in real terms between 2018 and 2023 despite inflation and population growth. Alberta and Newfoundland and Labrador were notable exceptions, reflecting fuel price volatility, capital replacement needs, and large infrastructure cost recovery. Newfoundland and Labrador demonstrates that hydroelectricity alone does not guarantee low electricity prices when major infrastructure costs must be recovered from a relatively small customer base.
  • The paper highlights growing pressure on electricity systems from electrification, industrial development, decarbonization policies, population growth, and emerging high-load sectors such as artificial intelligence. Provinces are increasingly investing in wind, solar, and battery storage, but legacy infrastructure, transmission constraints, and provincial policy choices continue to shape electricity costs. These pressures will make electricity pricing a more important economic and policy issue in the years ahead.

title: Granger Causality Regimes and Volatility Dynamics: A Unified Markov-Switching Framework

detail.title: Granger Causality Regimes and Volatility Dynamics: A Unified Markov-Switching Framework
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a Markov-switching vector autoregressive (MS-VAR) framework for analysing time-varying Granger causality in the presence of conditional heteroskedasticity. Existing approaches in the tradition of Psaradakis et al. (2005) embed both mean dynamics and covariance structure within the same regime indicators, creating a filter misattribution problem; volatility clusters and genuine causality regime changes are observationally similar from the perspective of the Hamilton filter, so the former can be spuriously attributed to the latter. The paper resolves this by separating the two channels, allowing regime switching only in the conditional mean while modelling second-moment dynamics through a state-invariant GARCH-DCC structure. Monte Carlo evidence for T ∈ {150, 300, 450} confirms that the fixed-covariance Markov-switching estimator produces substantially worse regime classification across all four predictive states, with mean classification error roughly four times as large as the proposed estimator at T = 300; differences are highly significant in Welch t-tests across all regimes and sample sizes. An empirical application to the trade-weighted U.S. dollar index and the Trade Policy Uncertainty (TPU) index of Baker et al. (2016) illustrates the practical importance of the approach: ARCH-LM tests strongly reject homoskedasticity in the VAR residuals, and the MS-VAR with GARCH-DCC uncovers four distinct predictive regimes whose timing maps cleanly onto the major episodes of U.S. trade policy history, from the Plaza Accord era and the China shock of the early 2000s to the two Trump trade-war episodes of 2017-2020 and 2025-2026, with TPU-driven dollar dynamics dominating in both trade-war periods and a persistent No Causality regime prevailing during intervals of broadly stable trade rules.

title: Model Starvation: Lindley's Revenge on R 2 , The Lasso, and Conformal Prediction
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, George Mason University and

detail.title: Model Starvation: Lindley's Revenge on R 2 , The Lasso, and Conformal Prediction
detail.abstract: We argue that variable selection in practice-fit a lasso, tune the penalty by cross-validation, read off a model by R 2-is model-starved: it picks a model without ever stating the decision the model must serve. Lindley [10] showed sixty years ago that the choice of variables is a decision problem whose answer depends on use, and that coefficient standard errors are irrelevant for prediction. We show that Lindley's prediction problem with variable-acquisition costs is exactly L 0-regularized least squares-spikeand-slab MAP with penalty λ = σ 2 e log{(1-θ)/θ}-computed at scale by Single Best Replacement [18]. The per-variable costs are precisely the local shrinkage scales of a global-local prior, so selection and shrinkage are one decision in two parameterizations; through the proximal/Tweedie bridge the horseshoe supplies its continuous, Bayes-risk-optimal form, and the same duality reads double descent. The diagnosis extends to conformal prediction, which delivers a coverage certificate but not the predictive kernel a decision requires. The cure is Lindley's: state the use, the loss, and the predictive distribution, then minimize expected loss.

title: Hold the Line Through 2035: A Strategy to Offset China’s Revisionist Actions and Sustain a Rules-based Order in the Asia-Pacific
affiliations: and Government of the United States of America - U.S. Naval War College

detail.title: Hold the Line Through 2035: A Strategy to Offset China’s Revisionist Actions and Sustain a Rules-based Order in the Asia-Pacific
detail.abstract: The 2020s represent the historical zenith of Beijing's capacity to mobilize national resources for domestic repression and external aggression. Consequently, the period leading up to 2035 marks a highly volatile "window of vulnerability" characterized by a heightened risk of kinetic conflict between the PRC and its regional neighbors, which directly threatens American security via treaty alliances and forward presence. Strategic ground ceded by the West during this timeframe is likely gone forever. Even if portions of the rules-based order could be salvaged later, the preventative defense of the existing system upfront remains substantially less costly than attempting to roll back revisionist gains down the road. If Washington appears to waver due to a premature overestimation of China's future economic and military trajectory, key regional partners will inevitably cut accommodationist deals with Beijing to protect their immediate interests.

title: Shifting the Frontier
affiliations: Total Portfolio Project

detail.title: Shifting the Frontier
detail.abstract: An Impact Frontier is the Pareto frontier between certainty-equivalent returns and expected change in an aggregate external outcome. This paper asks how that frontier shifts when the intervention is no longer an infinitesimal portfolio tilt by one investor. A finite investor coalition internalizes more of the equilibrium response it creates, so its optimal tilt is not generally the marginal investor's tilt scaled up. Government policy and stewardship act through different policy vectors: a government wedge changes the terms on which firms or margins are financed, while stewardship changes firm incentives where governance authority is available. In all three cases, the relevant policy vector is not the raw outcome score or a naive Pigouvian vector. It is the response-adjusted vector under the instrument's scope and cost. Separating market responses, policy rewards, and implementation costs makes investor coordination, government wedges, stewardship, and market-friction reductions comparable without treating them as interchangeable instruments.

title: Gender Pay Gap Reporting and Firm Outcomes: Evidence from the UK
affiliations: University of Bath - School of Management and University of Bath - School of Management

detail.title: Gender Pay Gap Reporting and Firm Outcomes: Evidence from the UK
detail.abstract: Gender pay inequality persists across labour markets, leading many governments to enact pay transparency legislation intended to narrow the gender pay gap by improving women's earnings. However, existing evidence shows that such legislation reduces the gender pay gap primarily through slower earnings growth for men rather than higher earnings for women. This paper examines the implications of this wage-compression mechanism for firm outcomes. Using a panel of UK firms (2018-2024) subject to gender pay gap reporting requirements, we estimate the association between publicly disclosed gender pay gaps and firm wage costs, productivity, turnover, and profitability. We find that narrowing gender pay gaps are associated with lower wage costs and lower productivity, but only in male-dominated firms. In contrast, narrowing gender pay gaps are associated with higher profitability only in female-dominated firms. Additional evidence suggests that this pattern is driven by gender asymmetry in firms' pay distributions with a concentration of men in the highest pay quartile, particularly in female-dominated firms. We find no evidence of an association between gender pay gaps and turnover, suggesting that the relationship between pay transparency and firm outcomes operates through internal wage-setting mechanisms rather than external demand-side channels. Overall, the results suggest that pay transparency legislation may create incentives for firms to respond through male wage compression rather than improvements in women's earnings.

title: ESG Risks and Private Equity Returns: New International Evidence
affiliations: , University of Alberta, University of South Carolina - Moore School of Business, Goethe University Frankfurt, House of Finance (HoF), Graduate School of Economics, Finance and Management (GSEFM), Students and Syracuse University - Whitman School of Management

detail.title: ESG Risks and Private Equity Returns: New International Evidence
detail.abstract: Using a sample of 23,563 privately held companies owned by 1,465 private equity funds from around the world, we provide evidence that fund returns are lower when the fund's portfolio companies are exposed to environmental, social and governance (ESG) risks. Although this negative risk-return relationship challenges the traditional finance axiom that returns compensate for risk, we explain our results using institutional theory from the international business literature. Failure to comply with formal and informal ESG institutions undermines the normative legitimacy of portfolio companies, resulting in lower returns at the fund level through normative sanctioning. A higher cultural distance of a fund's headquarters from its portfolio companies (our measure of liability of foreignness) exacerbates the return penalty for earlystage venture funds (due to their liability of newness), but mitigates it for later-stage buyout funds. Limited cognitive or regulative legitimacy, due to investments in early-stage venture companies or countries with poor formal ESG institutions, exacerbates the negative effect of ESG risk-taking on fund returns, driven by a strong reliance on normative legitimacy. Reduced reliance on normative legitimacy, as seen in "sin"-sectors, mitigates the valuation effect. Finally, normative sanctioning is stronger as more economic and financial resources are available. Our study makes a contribution to the international business literature by linking research on crossborder private equity and sustainability. It also provides important practical insights.

title: Algorithm in the AI and Digital Economy
affiliations: and Tsinghua University - Institute of Economics

detail.title: Algorithm in the AI and Digital Economy
detail.abstract: As artificial intelligence becomes a central engine of modern economic growth, standard macroeconomic frameworks must evolve to conceptualize algorithms not merely as decision rules, but as multidimensional technologies subject to strict computational constraints. This paper develops a novel endogenous growth model bridging theoretical computer science and macroeconomics, characterizing algorithmic innovation through the intrinsic trade-off between time complexity (compute utilization efficiency) and space complexity (memory utilization efficiency). We establish a unique asymptotic Balanced Growth Path (BGP) where, despite exploding data privacy costs, the economy sustains growth by directing innovation exclusively toward time-complexity optimization. The framework provides a formal macroeconomic foundation for "Wirth's Law,'' demonstrating that rapid exogenous hardware progress (Moore's Law) actively crowds out algorithmic R&D. Furthermore, we show that sudden algorithmic breakthroughs generate an ambiguous short-run effect on hardware demand but unambiguously increase long-run demand, explaining recent financial market dynamics as a computational Jevons Paradox. Normative analysis reveals that decentralized markets systematically under-invest in algorithmic innovation due to classic monopoly distortions and a novel "over-reaction to hardware growth.'' Finally, we demonstrate that when the economy collides with an aggregate energy bottleneck, physical hardware scaling halts, fully reversing Wirth's Law and inducing an explosive reallocation of labor into algorithmic R&D as the sole engine of long-run growth.

title: Estimating the Demand for a Digital Euro: A Survey Approach for France, Germany and Italy
affiliations: University of Marburg - School of Business & Economics, University of Trier - Faculty of Economics and University of Trier - Faculty of Economics

detail.title: Estimating the Demand for a Digital Euro: A Survey Approach for France, Germany and Italy

declarations.ethicsApproval: The survey was preregistered, and the underlying hypotheses were described in the AEA RCT registry on 20 October 2023 (RCT ID AEARCTR-0012329: Attitudes Towards and Demand for a Digital Euro: A Representative Survey in France, Germany, and Italy; https://www.socialscienceregistry.org/trials/12329).

detail.abstract: This paper analyses the extensive and intensive margins of demand for a retail digital euro. We conducted a representative survey in France, Germany and Italy in November-December 2023. We find that 52-62% of respondents are willing to hold a digital euro, depending on the interest rate spread, with a higher share in Italy than in France or Germany. Design features (cash-like vs deposit-like) appear to play only a very limited role. Average demand depends on the hypothetical interest rate spread relative to current accounts and ranges from EUR 700 to EUR 1,100, implying an aggregate demand of 1.5-2.5% of GDP. Willingness to hold a digital euro is associated with socio-demographic factors, trust in the ECB and the EU, digitalisation and payment behaviour. Negative interest rate spreads relative to current accounts reduce willingness to hold the digital euro more strongly than positive spreads increase it. Behavioural characteristics tend to be correlated with the likelihood of adoption, whereas economic factors, particularly income and interest rates, are mainly related to the level of demand. This distinction becomes more pronounced when conditioning on positive demand, suggesting that socio-demographic factors primarily influence participation decisions rather than quantities demanded.

title: The Pattern-Causality Matrix for Directed Dependence in Nonlinear Time Series
affiliations: Monash University - Department of Econometrics & Business Statistics, University of Edinburgh Business School and Monash University - Department of Econometrics & Business Statistics

detail.title: The Pattern-Causality Matrix for Directed Dependence in Nonlinear Time Series
detail.abstract: The pattern-causality (PC) matrix shows how a directed relation between nonlinear time series is expressed locally. Most methods compress the relation into a single number; the PC matrix instead decomposes local responses into positive, negative, and mixed-pattern (dark) classes, laid out as a heatmap that can be read, summarized numerically, and computed for all ordered pairs in a multivariate system. We build the matrix from delay embedding, nearest-neighbor projection following Farmer & Sidorowich (1987), and a signature-to-pattern map, and we equip it with a timeseries-aware assessment layer: block-based stability summaries, a null-calibrated detection rule, and a common-driver diagnostic that flags shared-driver-induced pairwise structure. Earlier work introduced pattern causality and showed empirical reach across finance, ecology, and neurology; here we make the matrix the object of study and give it a computational and statistical formulation. In controlled experiments it recovers designed structure, concentrating mass in the positive class under aligned dynamics and in the negative class under sign-reversing dynamics, with detection at the calibrated floor under an independent null. Applied to climate indices and residual stock returns, the matrix reveals local sign structure that scalar directed-dependence scores cannot reveal. The CRAN package patterncausality and reproducibility scripts regenerate every result.

title: Safety-Guided Deep Reinforcement Learning for Magnetic Microrobot Navigation and Precision Drug Delivery in Complex Vascular Networks
affiliations: Al Adan Hospital, American International University Kuwait and American International University Kuwait

detail.title: Safety-Guided Deep Reinforcement Learning for Magnetic Microrobot Navigation and Precision Drug Delivery in Complex Vascular Networks
detail.abstract: Magnetic microrobots are a promising approach for targeted drug delivery because they can be remotely guided toward localized therapeutic regions while reducing non-specific drug distribution. However, autonomous navigation in vascular environments remains difficult because of branching vessel structures, wall collision risks, misleading blood flow directions, target-location uncertainty, actuation disturbance, and restrictive vessel geometry. This study proposed a Safety-Guided Proximal Policy Optimization Deep Reinforcement Learning framework for magnetic microrobot navigation and target-zone drug delivery in simulated vascular networks. The proposed method combines a PPO-based navigation policy with a local magnetic safety-guidance layer that evaluates candidate actions, rejects unsafe movements, and selects vessel-aware, target-directed steering actions. A two-dimensional branching vascular environment was developed with randomized target placement, stochastic blood flow disturbance, collision constraints, misleading non-target branches, and automatic drug release upon entry into the target delivery radius. The framework was evaluated under progressively challenging scenarios, including standard conditions, moderate disturbance, high disturbance, and severe narrow vessel stress. The proposed method achieved 97.50% success under moderate disturbance, 87.50% success under high disturbance, and 69.17% success under severe narrow-vessel stress, showing realistic performance degradation as the environmental difficulty increased. Compared with the centerline, greedy direct, passive flow-following, and random baselines, the proposed framework maintained a stronger target-delivery performance and lower collision rates. These findings demonstrate that safety-guided reinforcement learning can improve the robustness of magnetic microrobot navigation in constrained vascular drug delivery simulations.

title: Cognitive Morphology And Lexical Acquisition: Deconstructing The Etymological Paradigm In High-Stakes Administrative Examinations

detail.title: Cognitive Morphology And Lexical Acquisition: Deconstructing The Etymological Paradigm In High-Stakes Administrative Examinations
detail.abstract: For years, Indian competitive exams-especially the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) Civil Services Examination-have leaned almost entirely on rote memorization. This paper takes a hard look at a different linguistic method: learning through morphological parsing and etymological deduction. The central question here is: What really happens when students move from passively memorizing lists to actively breaking down word structure? The research explores how understanding a word's origins builds tough, lasting "cognitive maps" in the learner's memory. Concrete teaching tools like Prefix-Root-Suffix matrices and deduction from contextual clues show a clear drop in mental strain during high-pressure situations. The discussion also doesn't shy away from the limits of this method, like issues of words drifting in meaning or not being totally transparent. At the end, the paper puts forward an independent synthesis: true mastery of administrative language comes from weaving together the rigorous logic of etymology with real-world awareness of word pairings and context, creating a powerful vocabulary toolkit for future public administrators.

title: Diving into the Unknown Unknowns: Collective Action under Different Degrees of Uncertainty
affiliations: and Arizona State University (ASU)

detail.title: Diving into the Unknown Unknowns: Collective Action under Different Degrees of Uncertainty

declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by a U.S. National Science Foundation grant (account GR 39387).

detail.abstract: Uncertainty plays a crucial role in economic decision-making and can be categorized into risk, ambiguity, and "unknown unknowns" based on the subject's level of knowledge. In an incentivized one-shot linear public goods game with 800 U.S. citizens, we introduce these types of uncertainty regarding the potential destruction of the public good in a between-subject design. Specifically, we split risk into two degrees as to capture more nuanced differences of uncertainty-namely simple and compound risk-and thus implement four treatment conditions. While participants in the condition RISK_SIMPLE know the exact probability of destruction, and those in RISK_COMPOUND know its discrete uniform distribution, participants in AMBIGUITY only learn about the destruction possibility, and those in UNKNOWN UNKNOWNS are only informed that an unspecified event may occur and that the setting is dangerous. Our results show that collective action efforts are significantly different when uncertainty takes on the type of unknown unknowns: we find higher levels of cooperation and more pronounced cooperative beliefs compared to the risky and ambiguous environments.

title: Balancing Development and Environmental Protection in India: The Role of Law, Policy, and the Judiciary

detail.title: Balancing Development and Environmental Protection in India: The Role of Law, Policy, and the Judiciary
detail.abstract: Environmental governance-the institutional arrangements for making decisions-across various sectors: water and air pollution, infrastructure projects, climate negotiations, and the associated environmental jurisprudence in India, formally institutionalised over the last four decades following the Stockholm Conference. Since then, it has increasingly confronted tensions between development-led growth and a rights-oriented judicial discourse. Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India (2000) remains one of the first famous judicial engagements.

title: Twice-Told Preferences: Reliability, Repeated Elicitation, and Household Wealth

detail.title: Twice-Told Preferences: Reliability, Repeated Elicitation, and Household Wealth
detail.abstract: Elicited preferences are measured noisily and usually only once, so their estimated links to behavior are attenuated. Using two Japanese household panels that re-ask an identical money-earlier-or-later question annually for fourteen years, I measure the attenuation and remove it. Wave-to-wave reliability is one-half while the persistent component decays by only two percent a year, so averaging a household’s answers, or instrumenting one wave with another, roughly doubles the discount-rate coeﬀicient. A one-standard-deviation increase in impatience predicts about 43% lower financial wealth and a 5.4-percentage-point lower probability of holding securities, twice the single-wave estimate. The gradient survives income, education, and financial-literacy controls, and the discarded variation looks like survey noise, not a moving required rate of return.

title: Four Paths to Hilbert's Eighth Problem
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Four Paths to Hilbert's Eighth Problem
detail.abstract: We place the generalized gamma convolution (GGC) reformulation of the Riemann Hypothesis (RH) within the wider landscape of "real-zeros" programs-Pólya-de Bruijn-Newman, Lee-Yang/Cardon, Jensen polynomials, and van Dantzig-Wald-and, in light of recent work (Rodgers-Tao 2020; Konstantopoulos-Patie-Sarkar 2024), identify the most promising path. Three theses organise the paper. First, RH is a single positivity statement in four equivalent costumes: a Pick (Nevanlinna) condition, a complete-monotonicity (Thorin) condition, the de Bruijn-Newman value Λ dBN = 0, and van Dantzig membership of ξ in the Laguerre-Pólya class. Second, the algebraic operations native to the GGC and Wald frameworks-subordination, Esscher tilting, and Fourier/Möbius resummation-are provably incapable of supplying that positivity: they preserve or relabel it, never generate it. Third, the generative front is the Lee-Yang/Cardon construction, anchored by the unconditional von Mangoldt positivity that distinguishes ξ from Pólya's counterexample. We keep two tiers strictly separate throughout-an unconditional (subordinator) tier and an RH-equivalent (GGC) tier-and we make no claim to prove RH; the contribution is a map of the terrain and a program with explicit partial targets.

title: When Waiting is Not a Price: Court-Processing Timing and Medical Utilization in Pretrial Detention
affiliations: UC Berkeley,  and UC Berkeley

detail.title: When Waiting is Not a Price: Court-Processing Timing and Medical Utilization in Pretrial Detention
detail.abstract: Waiting is often treated as a price or screen. We study a different form of administrative burden: delay generated by imperfect synchronization between courts and jails. Using Cook County jail records, we exploit weekend booking as quasi-experimental variation in detainees’ position relative to a weekday court-movement calendar. Among detainees held at least 60 days, an additional 24 hours before the first recorded court-related custody movement increases subsequent medical encounters by about 4 percent, with no detectable effects on incidents, infractions, or housing moves. Coordination burdens can shift costs across public institutions without revealing social need.

title: Abstraction Contracts and Report-Level Non-Determinacy of Exploitability Claims

detail.title: Abstraction Contracts and Report-Level Non-Determinacy of Exploitability Claims
detail.abstract: Reports under game abstraction often provide a reported abstract object R = (G ′ , σ ′): an abstract game and an abstract behavior-strategy profile. Such a report is not itself an originalgame behavior profile. Consequently, an exploitability claim reported only as R is not checkable from what is reported: the lifting rule can change the original-game profile being evaluated. The remedy is direct: disclose the abstraction contract C = (G, G ′ , ϕ, λ, ρ, E), not only the abstract report. This note isolates the mechanism in a hand-checkable witness. The reported strategy assigns positive probability to two abstract actions, X and Y. Two contracts share the same G, G ′ , fixed many-to-one map ϕ, σ ′ , inert ρ, and evaluation E; their liftings λ 1 and λ 2 are both ϕ-compatible, so ϕ # (λ i (σ ′)) = σ ′. Nevertheless the induced original-game exploitability values are 2.0 and 4.0. The result is a minimal theorem/reproducibility note about report-level auditability.

title: Comparing Data Envelopment Analysis and Stochastic Frontier Analysis for Measuring Odi Bowler Efficiency

detail.title: Comparing Data Envelopment Analysis and Stochastic Frontier Analysis for Measuring Odi Bowler Efficiency
detail.abstract: Background: Traditional cricket bowling indicators such as wickets, economy rate and runs conceded provide useful but incomplete signals of player performance. Efficiency methods can evaluate how bowlers convert available inputs into wicket-taking outputs while also recognising performance variation across match contexts. Purpose: This study measures the relative efficiency of One Day International bowlers in the 2022 season and compares Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) with Stochastic Frontier Analysis (SFA) as alternative analytical approaches. Methods: Secondary performance data for ODI bowlers were analysed using DEA and SFA. DEA models compared variable returns to scale (VRS) and constant returns to scale (CRS) output-oriented specifications, while SFA compared half-normal efficiency estimates under Jondrow-Lovell-Materov-Schmidt and Battese-Coelli estimators. Results: The VRS DEA model produced a mean efficiency score of 49.35 percent and identified six efficient bowlers, while the CRS model produced a lower mean efficiency score of 17.60 percent. Within SFA, the Battese-Coelli half-normal model generated a higher mean efficiency score of 65.41 percent than the Jondrow-Lovell-Materov-Schmidt half-normal estimate of 64.89 percent. The selected SFA model identified Ebadot Hossain as the most efficient bowler in the analysed sample, with an efficiency score of 93.69 percent. Conclusion: SFA offered the more suitable final framework for this dataset because it incorporated stochastic noise and provided stronger efficiency differentiation, while VRS was preferred within the DEA family.

title: INTERPOL’s Jurisdiction over Transnational Commercial Crimes Between Prosecuting Financial Fraud and Preventing the Misuse of Red Notices in Civil Disputes
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: INTERPOL’s Jurisdiction over Transnational Commercial Crimes Between Prosecuting Financial Fraud and Preventing the Misuse of Red Notices in Civil Disputes
detail.abstract: This article examines INTERPOL’s constitutional competence in addressing transnational commercial and financial crimes, particularly fraud, money laundering, and cross-border embezzlement. While Article 2 of the INTERPOL Constitution provides a legitimate basis for international police cooperation against “ordinary-law crime,” serious legal concerns arise when Red Notices are misused in disputes that are essentially civil or contractual in nature.The study highlights the fundamental distinction between criminal commercial fraud and private commercial conflicts, analyzes the adverse human rights consequences of wrongful Red Notices, and emphasizes the oversight role of the Commission for the Control of INTERPOL’s Files (CCF) as an institutional safeguard against abuse. The article concludes by proposing reforms aimed at strengthening evidentiary standards, enhancing transparency, and preventing INTERPOL mechanisms from being transformed into tools of commercial coercion.

title: Information in (and not in) Interest Rate Surveys
affiliations: University of York - Department of Economics and Related Studies and University of York

detail.title: Information in (and not in) Interest Rate Surveys
detail.abstract: We develop a joint shadow rate term structure model for zero-coupon yields and survey expectations that allows for departures between subjective and objective expectations, arising from biases both in perceived policy responses and in expectations of fundamentals. Using U.S. data, we find evidence of both: reaction function errors at short maturities and probability forecast errors at long maturities. These biases have three main implications. First, not accounting for survey biases can distort inference about the dynamics of observed interest rates. Second, surveys are essential to recover the premium perceived by investors. Third, survey-implied term premia are systematically lower than those inferred from bond prices.

title: Mapping the Hidden Burden: A Geospatial Analysis of Environmental And Social Determinants and Their Association with Pancreatic Cancer Incidence and Mortality in the United States
affiliations: University of Alabama at Birmingham, University of Alabama at Birmingham, University of Alabama at Birmingham, University of Alabama at Birmingham, University of Alabama at Birmingham, University of Alabama at Birmingham, University of Alabama at Birmingham - Institute for Cancer Outcomes and Survivorship, University of Alabama at Birmingham, University of Alabama and University of Alabama at Birmingham - Department of Pediatrics

detail.title: Mapping the Hidden Burden: A Geospatial Analysis of Environmental And Social Determinants and Their Association with Pancreatic Cancer Incidence and Mortality in the United States

declarations.declarationOfInterest: All Authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for this article.

detail.abstract:
Background: Prior studies have shown substantial regional variation in pancreatic cancer incidence and mortality. Understanding how environmental exposures and social vulnerability shape these geographic patterns may reveal actionable drivers of disease burden.

Methods: County-level incidence and mortality data (2017–2022) were obtained from the NIH State Cancer Profiles and CDC Environmental Public Health Tracking Network. Age-adjusted rates were linked with environmental (particulate matter (PM₂.₅), arsenic), behavioral (smoking, obesity, binge drinking), and social vulnerability (social vulnerability index[ SVI]) metrics. Spatial autocorrelation (Global Moran’s I) and hotspot analysis (Getis-Ord Gi*) were performed in ArcGIS Pro. Linear regression, SVI domain decomposition, and urban–rural interaction modeling was conducted to evaluate regional associations between social and environmental determinants and pancreatic cancer incidence and mortality (or whatever you want it to say here). Geographically weighted regression (GWR) assessed regional heterogeneity.

Results: Among 3,143 U.S. counties, the national median age-adjusted incidence rate was 13.8 per 100,000 (IQR 12.4–15.3), with significant spatial clustering (Moran's I = 0.47, p < 0.001). Incidence hotspots concentrated in the Deep South, Appalachia, and the industrial Midwest. Median age-adjusted mortality was 7.65 per 100,000 (IQR 0.0–12.2; Moran's I = 0.42, p < 0.001), extending into Arkansas, Tennessee, and the Carolinas. Counties with elevated mortality showed disproportionately higher social vulnerability and environmental exposures. In multivariable analyses (n = 1,683 counties), incidence was independently associated with PM₂.₅ (β = 0.87, p < 0.001) and obesity (β = 0.79, p < 0.001). Mortality was independently associated with SVI (β = 5.18, p < 0.001), PM₂.₅ (β = 0.46, p < 0.001), and alcohol consumption (β = 13.59, p = 0.014). The model explained 16–18% of geographic variance.

Conclusion: Pancreatic cancer burden clusters in distinct regions due to intersecting environmental, behavioral factors and SVI.

title: The Impact of U.S. Critical Audit Matter Disclosure on Firms' Credit Ratings
affiliations: Queen's University Belfast - Queen's Management School and Queen's University Belfast

detail.title: The Impact of U.S. Critical Audit Matter Disclosure on Firms' Credit Ratings
detail.abstract:
Purpose – This paper examines the informativeness of U.S. critical audit matter (CAM) disclosure to credit rating agencies (CRAs) as sophisticated beneficiaries of audited financial statements. It investigates the impact of CAM disclosure—mandated by the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) to highlight high-risk areas—on firms’ credit ratings.

Design/methodology/approach – We conduct multivariate analysis of CAM effects on a firm’s credit rating through ologit regressions (credit rating analysis), logit models (investment versus speculative-grade analysis), intertemporal (within-firm) change analyses, and quasi-experimental difference-in-differences specifications. We conduct our tests using a sample of U.S. companies that adopt CAM disclosures and employ both a control group of nonadopters and a propensity score-matched group of economically comparable nonadopters. Main tests use S&P long-term issuer credit ratings, with additional robustness checks utilizing Fitch ratings.

Findings – After controlling for firm characteristics and corporate governance attributes, we document that CAM disclosure negatively affects firms’ credit ratings. Our results are robust to endogeneity concerns and various estimation procedures, providing novel evidence that the new requirement of CAM disclosure is associated with significant consequences for preparers and users of financial reports, particularly regarding credit rating assessments.

Originality – This research advances the literature on expanded audit reports by providing the first empirical evidence that CAM disclosures are informative to CRAs, bridging the gap between studies focused on market reactions and those on experimental assessments of audit information. It highlights the direct impact of CAM disclosures on credit ratings, supporting the usefulness of expanded auditor reporting for sophisticated users of financial statements.

Practical implications – The evidence-based insights from this study demonstrate that CAM disclosures have significant implications for credit risk assessments, making them relevant to auditors, preparers and users of financial reports, policymakers and regulatory bodies, specifically the PCAOB, Financial Reporting Council (FRC), and International Auditing and Assurance Standard Board (IAASB).

title: Exchange Rate Predictability from Monetary Policy Path Expectations: Evidence from OIS Slopes
affiliations: Yokohama City University and Yokohama City University - Graduate School of International Management

detail.title: Exchange Rate Predictability from Monetary Policy Path Expectations: Evidence from OIS Slopes
detail.abstract: This paper studies how revisions in expected monetary policy paths affect exchange rates. We construct a slope factor from one-month and twelve-month Overnight Index Swap (OIS) rates to capture policy-path news embedded in short-term interest rate markets. Using weekly data from 2008 to 2025, we show that increases in the U.S. slope predict subsequent appreciations of the U.S. dollar, consistent with the role of U.S. monetary policy as a global anchor for financial markets. This predictability weakens during high-attention periods, such as FOMC weeks, suggesting that policy-path information is incorporated more rapidly into exchange rates when market attention is elevated. We further examine the role of central bank communication by constructing a text-based Hawk-Dove Index from FOMC speeches. A more hawkish speech tone is associated with a flattening of the U.S. slope, reflecting a stronger response of one-month OIS rates than twelve-month OIS rates. We interpret these findings using a simple framework with time-varying information frictions, in which policy-path news is incorporated gradually in normal periods but more rapidly during high-attention events.

title: The Varoka Multiplier

detail.title: The Varoka Multiplier

detail.abstract: This paper introduces version 3.0 of the Varoka Multiplier-formally, the Varoka Compound Efficiency Theory-an eight-factor analytical framework for measuring the structural competitive advantage of emerging economies in technology-intensive production. I argue that the cost gap practitioners observe between countries like China and the United States is not a single-variable story. It is a compound. When wage differentials, currency undervaluation, talent depth, execution speed, energy cost, data liquidity, capital efficiency, and ecosystem density all act on the same dollar at once, the result is not addition. It is multiplication. The eight factors-α (wage ratio), β (PPP amplification), γ (talent density), δ (execution speed), ε (energy cost inverse), ζ (data liquidity), κ (capital efficiency), and η (ecosystem density) are each independently measurable using publicly available data. I weight the product by an output-quality adjustment Q and divide by a risk-drag denominator R, producing what I call the Net Varoka Multiplier (VM₃). Applied to the China-United States technology labor market in 2026, the framework yields a gross multiplier of approximately 17x and a risk-adjusted, decorrelated multiplier of roughly 10x meaning each dollar invested in an integrated engineering stack in China generates 10 to 17 dollars of comparable productive capacity in the United States. A parallel India-U.S. estimate (~8x gross, ~5x decorrelated) demonstrates that the framework discriminates correctly between sectors and geographies. I close with a discussion of why artificial intelligence reinforces, rather than neutralises, this compound-and what that means for the next decade of global competition.

title: Divergent Minds, Convergent Baselines: A Bounded-Rationality Account of LLM-Human Strategic Behaviour

detail.title: Divergent Minds, Convergent Baselines: A Bounded-Rationality Account of LLM-Human Strategic Behaviour

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests. The research was conducted independently and does not evaluate or promote any specific commercial product.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This research is purely theoretical and involves no human or animal subjects. The empirical evidence cited is drawn from published academic literature
